domains.name: Citation & Referencing
domains.summary: Citation is both a technical system and a rhetorical practice. This domain moves from why and when academics cite, through the mechanics of the main referencing systems (author–date, numeric and note-based), locators and reference lists, to the rhetorical functions of citation and how these vary across disciplines. Formatting is treated as learnable and checkable, ideally with reference-management tools, so that teaching time goes to the harder judgements: what needs citing, whether a cited source really supports the claim, how citation positions the writer, and what disciplinary readers expect.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why and when to cite, how to format citations and reference lists accurately in the system your department or journal uses, and how expert writers use citation to build and position their own arguments.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Reasons for citing, when citation is needed, and accurate author–date (or departmental) formatting for books, articles and web pages.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Consistent use of one system across an extended source-based assignment, with locators, reference lists and systematic accuracy checks that often feed into progression decisions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Switching to the department's prescribed system, citing a wider range of source types, and beginning to use citation for more than attribution.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Using citation to compare, evaluate and link sources in critical reviews and dissertations, and matching the citation norms of the discipline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Switching between journal styles, managing large reference libraries accurately, and using citation to position a contribution within a field.

domains.name: Generative AI Literacy
domains.summary: Generative AI literacy is treated here as part of academic literacy: understanding how large language models generate text and why they fail; reading and applying AI policies that vary by institution, module and task; acknowledging and verifying AI use; and using AI in ways that build rather than replace learners' own language, reasoning and voice. The domain also covers the limits of AI-text detection, including documented bias against writers using English as an additional language, and privacy and intellectual-property risks. Tools and policies change quickly, so topics are framed around durable principles and verification habits rather than particular products.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how generative AI tools work and where they fail, and how to find out what AI use is allowed in each task. You will also practise acknowledging and checking AI use, using AI to develop your English while keeping your own voice, and responding if a detector wrongly flags your work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: How generative AI works and fails, finding the AI rules for each task, and using AI for explanation and practice rather than to produce assessed text.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Transparent, policy-compliant AI use in source-based assignments, verifying outputs and references, and keeping evidence of one's own writing process.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Module-specific rules, acknowledging use, and evaluating AI as a language and study resource within the discipline.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: AI in literature searching and summarising, authorship and voice in extended writing, and data privacy in dissertation research.
stageEmphasis.pgr: AI research tools, publisher and funder policies, research data privacy and intellectual property, and authorship norms in publication.

domains.name: Academic Integrity
domains.summary: Academic integrity is taught here as values and practices rather than a list of offences. The domain moves from shared values and an informed understanding of plagiarism (including the developmental status of patchwriting and the contested role of intention) to collusion, contract cheating, reuse of one's own work and research integrity, and to the procedural knowledge learners need: interpreting similarity reports, navigating policies and processes, and managing pressure without shortcuts. Rules differ between institutions and modules, so teaching centres on locating and reading the rules that apply, and similarity scores are never treated as verdicts.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what academic integrity means in practice, how to avoid plagiarism, collusion and other misconduct, what similarity reports do and do not show, where to get help when deadlines and pressure build up, and what your rights are if questions are ever raised about your work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Values, a clear and non-threatening understanding of plagiarism and collusion, and where to get help, introduced early in the course.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Integrity in source-based writing, similarity reports as formative tools, and the policies that will govern the degree programme.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Department-specific rules on collaboration, reuse of work and lab or project data, and strategies for managing workload pressure.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation to regulations, reuse of prior work, group-assessment boundaries, and integrity in dissertation research and data.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Research integrity, text recycling in theses and publications, authorship, and the codes of conduct governing research.

topics.name: Why academics cite
topics.description: Explain the purposes citation serves in academic writing: giving credit, letting readers verify and follow up claims, showing how a text joins an ongoing scholarly conversation, and positioning the writer in relation to other work. Seeing citation as communicative rather than only as a rule for avoiding penalties underpins every later decision about what, when and how to cite.
masteryEvidence: Names at least three distinct purposes of citation (credit, verifiability, joining a conversation, supporting or positioning a claim) and illustrates each from a model text
Explains, for a given citation in a short extract, what a reader would lose if it were removed
Distinguishes the communicative reasons for citing from avoiding penalties when discussing their own writing
Describes citation as a way of displaying reading and building credibility with an expert reader such as a marker
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a 120-word paragraph from a textbook or student exemplar with its three citations removed, and ask what a lecturer reading it would question or be unable to check. Strong answers go beyond 'it would be plagiarism' to verifiability, credit and the strength of the claims; weak answers mention only rules or penalties.

topics.name: When to cite
topics.description: Decide which content requires citation (others' specific ideas, findings, data, wording, visuals, frameworks and lines of argument) and which does not (the writer's own analysis and genuinely common knowledge). Because common knowledge is relative to discipline, readership and level of study, learners need a working procedure for doubtful cases rather than a fixed list.
masteryEvidence: Classifies statements in a short text as requiring citation, common knowledge for the intended reader, or the writer's own contribution, and justifies borderline decisions
Cites sources for statistics, findings, definitions, visuals and paraphrased ideas, not only for quotations
Applies a doubt procedure to unclear cases (for example: would my reader ask where this comes from, and did I learn it from a particular source for this task?)
Explains that what counts as common knowledge differs between disciplines, readerships and levels of study
Leaves the writer's own inferences and conclusions uncited while signalling clearly that they are the writer's
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give ten statements on a topic the learner has read about (a statistic, a date widely taught at school, a named theory, a contested causal claim, the learner's own inference from two sources, and so on) and ask them to mark each 'cite', 'no need' or 'depends', with a reason. Look for reasons tied to the reader, the specificity of the claim and the discipline rather than rules such as 'cite every sentence'.

topics.name: Referencing systems and style guides
topics.description: Distinguish the main families of referencing system — author–date (APA 7, Chicago author–date, Harvard variants), MLA's author–page system, numeric (IEEE, Vancouver) and note-based (Chicago notes and bibliography, OSCOLA) — and recognise that the departmental, module or journal guide, not a universal rule, decides which applies. 'Harvard' has no single authoritative edition, so learners must follow the version their institution specifies.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the system family used in an unfamiliar text from its in-text citations and reference list or notes
Locates and follows the style guide specified in an assignment brief, module handbook or journal's author guidelines
Explains that Harvard is a family of institutional variants rather than one published standard, and checks which version applies
Relates a system's design to what it foregrounds for the reader (author and date, sequence and compactness, or pinpointing and commentary in notes)
Keeps to one system consistently within a document
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give four short extracts with their reference lists or notes (APA, MLA, IEEE, OSCOLA) and ask the learner to name each system family, say where they would find its authoritative rules, and identify one distinguishing feature. Check in particular whether they treat 'Harvard' as one fixed standard.

topics.name: In-text citation: author–date
topics.description: Format author–date in-text citations accurately in narrative and parenthetical forms — one, two and three or more authors, et al., group authors, several works in one citation, same-author same-year works and secondary citation — following the specified guide (usually APA 7 or an institutional Harvard). Accurate, well-placed in-text citation lets readers move without friction from a claim to its reference entry and see exactly which content is attributed.
masteryEvidence: Formats narrative and parenthetical citations correctly for one, two and three or more authors in the specified guide
Applies the guide's rules on et al., ampersand versus 'and', and group-author abbreviations
Orders several works within one parenthesis and distinguishes same-author same-year works with letter suffixes
Places each citation so that the reader can tell which claim it supports, including mid-sentence where only part of a sentence is attributed
Formats a secondary citation as the guide requires and matches every citation to a reference entry
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write three sentences citing (a) a single-author source narratively, (b) two three-author sources together in one parenthesis, and (c) a group author on first mention with its abbreviation. Check format against the specified guide, the order of works, and whether each citation's position matches the attributed content.

topics.name: Numeric citation systems
topics.description: Use numeric systems such as IEEE and Vancouver: number sources in order of first citation, reuse a source's number when citing it again, format bracketed or superscript numbers, multiple citations and ranges, and compile the reference list in numerical order. Numeric styles dominate engineering, computing and much of medicine, where cited authors usually stay in the background and naming them is a deliberate choice.
masteryEvidence: Assigns numbers in order of first citation and reuses the original number for repeat citations
Formats single, multiple and range citations as the specified style requires
Compiles a reference list in citation order, not alphabetical order, with entries formatted to the specified style
Names authors alongside the number only when the author matters for contrast, credit or evaluation
Keeps numbering correct after reordering or deleting text, normally by using a reference manager
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 150-word paragraph in IEEE style in which two sources are numbered out of sequence and one repeated source has been given a new number. Ask the learner to correct the numbering and reorder the reference list, and to say where the IEEE rules are published. Check sequence, reuse of numbers and list order.

topics.name: Note-based citation
topics.description: Use footnote or endnote systems — Chicago notes and bibliography and, in UK law, OSCOLA — formatting full and shortened notes, pinpoint references, subsequent references and, where required, a bibliography or tables of cases and legislation. Notes are the norm in history, much of the humanities and law; they can also carry brief discursive commentary, which must be kept distinct from citation and from the main argument.
masteryEvidence: Places note reference numbers correctly in relation to punctuation and the attributed material, following the specified guide
Formats a full first note and later shortened notes for the same source, applying the guide's current rule on repeated citations
Gives pinpoint references to the specific page, paragraph or section relied on
Formats legal authorities (cases, legislation) according to OSCOLA where required and distinguishes them from secondary sources
Compiles a bibliography, and tables of authorities where required, consistent with the notes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner records for a book, a journal article and, for law students, a reported case. Ask for a full first note, a shortened subsequent note citing a different page, and the bibliography entries. Check the differences between note and bibliography formats, pinpoints, and consistency with the named guide.

topics.name: Compiling a reference list
topics.description: Build reference-list entries from their core elements — who, when, what and where, including DOIs or stable URLs — for the source types most often cited, and order, format and label the list as the specified guide requires. Learners need to identify the source type and locate the elements in the source itself rather than copy entries from search results or model lists.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the source type (journal article, book, chapter in an edited book, report, web page) and locates each required element in the source
Formats entries with correct element order, punctuation, italics and capitalisation, such as sentence case for article titles in APA
Formats DOIs and URLs as the guide requires and omits elements the current edition no longer requires
Orders entries correctly for the system and applies consistent layout such as hanging indents
Includes every cited source and excludes uncited reading unless a bibliography is requested
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the first page of a journal article and the title, copyright and contents pages of an edited book, and ask for reference entries for the article and for one chapter. Check that the chapter is distinguished from the book, editors are formatted as editors, and the article's capitalisation and DOI are correct.

topics.name: Citing diverse source types
topics.description: Cite sources beyond books and journal articles — web pages, reports and other grey literature, datasets, software, standards, audiovisual material, social media, personal communications and outputs of generative AI tools — by identifying who is responsible, which version was used, when, and how a reader can retrieve it. Where the reader cannot retrieve a source, learners follow how their guide and institution handle it rather than inventing a format.
masteryEvidence: Identifies author (including organisational authors), date, title, version and retrieval information for an unfamiliar source and adapts the closest model in the guide
Cites datasets and software with version numbers and persistent identifiers where they exist
Gives timestamps or other locators when quoting or pinpointing audiovisual sources
Handles non-recoverable sources, such as personal communications and most AI conversations, as the specified guide and institution require
Includes retrieval dates only for content the guide treats as designed to change
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three unfamiliar items — a government web page with no named author, a versioned dataset in a repository, and a recorded conference talk — and ask the learner to cite each in-text and in the reference list in the specified guide. Look for correct identification of the responsible author, version or date and retrieval information, and a reasoned decision where the guide has no exact model.

topics.name: Page numbers and locators
topics.description: Give the precise location of cited material — page, paragraph, section, timestamp, table or figure — whenever quoting, when the guide requires or recommends it for paraphrase, and when pinpointing a specific claim in a long work. Locators let readers verify exactly what was taken from where; their form differs between systems and source types.
masteryEvidence: Includes a correctly formatted locator with every direct quotation in the specified guide
Uses paragraph numbers, section headings or timestamps for sources without page numbers
Adds locators to paraphrases of specific passages in long works where the guide recommends it or a reader would need it
Uses the printed page numbers of a published article rather than the page count of the PDF viewer
Formats page ranges and pinpoint references accurately, including in footnote systems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to cite (a) a quotation from page 47 of a book, (b) a quotation from an unpaginated web article, (c) a quotation from minute 12 of a recorded lecture, and (d) a paraphrase of one specific argument in a 300-page book. Check presence and form of each locator and the reasoning given for (d).

topics.name: Citation accuracy and consistency
topics.description: Check that every in-text citation has a matching reference entry and vice versa, that names, dates, titles, page ranges and identifiers are correct and consistently formatted, and that each cited source actually supports the claim attached to it. Reference-manager output, database exports and references produced by generative AI tools all need verifying against the source or an authoritative record.
masteryEvidence: Cross-checks in-text citations against the reference list in both directions and resolves every mismatch in names, spelling and year
Verifies bibliographic details and DOIs against the source or publisher record rather than relying on exported or generated metadata
Corrects typical reference-manager errors such as title-case titles, missing editors, duplicated entries and wrong item types
Returns to the source to confirm that it says what the text attributes to it, including any hedging or qualification
Applies one style consistently across citations, reference list, figure captions and appendices
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 250-word extract and reference list with six seeded errors: a missing reference, a misspelt author, a year mismatch, a plausible but non-existent reference, an exported title in title case, and a claim the cited source does not make (supply that source's abstract). Allow ten minutes. The non-existent reference and the misrepresented claim best separate thorough checkers from those who check format only.

topics.name: Rhetorical functions of citation
topics.description: Recognise and use the range of functions citations perform — attribution, exemplification, pointing to further reading, statement of use, application, evaluation, establishing links between sources, and comparing one's own findings with others' — and choose citation form and reporting language to fit the function. Using citation beyond simple attribution has been associated with more highly rated postgraduate writing.
masteryEvidence: Classifies the functions of citations in an expert text using a published typology and explains the writer's purpose in each case
Uses citations in their own writing to evaluate, to connect sources and to compare their own findings, not only to attribute
Selects integral or non-integral form and a reporting verb to match the intended function and stance
Revises a source-by-source descriptive paragraph so that its citations serve the writer's argument
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to label the function of each citation in a paragraph from their own draft, then rewrite the paragraph so that at least two citations do something other than attribute (for example evaluate, compare or link). Check whether labels are accurate and whether the rewrite changes the writer's role rather than only the wording.

topics.name: Disciplinary variation in citation
topics.description: Describe how citation practice differs across disciplines — in citation density, use of direct quotation, integral versus non-integral forms, reporting-verb choice and preferred systems — and relate these differences to how each field builds knowledge. Learners use this to read their own discipline's texts as models rather than applying one generic EAP template.
masteryEvidence: Analyses a small set of texts from their discipline for citation density, quotation, integral/non-integral ratio and reporting verbs
Explains how the patterns observed relate to the field's knowledge-making, such as cumulative findings versus interpretive debate
Adjusts their own citation practice to disciplinary expectations, for example by reducing direct quotation in a science report
Recognises variation within a discipline and between genres, such as review versus empirical articles or published versus student genres, and avoids overgeneralising
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two short extracts on related topics, one from a humanities or social science article and one from an engineering or life science article, and ask the learner to identify three differences in citation practice and propose a reason for each. Look for reasons connected to how knowledge is built in each field rather than stereotypes such as 'scientists don't like quotations'.

topics.name: How generative AI works and fails
topics.description: Explain in non-technical terms how large language models generate text — by predicting likely continuations from patterns learned from very large training datasets, with further tuning to follow instructions — and why this produces fluent but unverified output, fabricated facts and references, biases inherited from training data, and gaps beyond the training data. This understanding underpins every judgement about when AI output can be trusted and how it must be checked.
masteryEvidence: Explains that model output is generated from statistical patterns rather than retrieved from a verified database, and draws the implication for accuracy
Predicts tasks on which output is likely to be unreliable, such as specific references, recent events, specialised or local knowledge, exact quotations and calculations
Identifies one-sided framing or bias in an AI output and relates it to training data
Distinguishes tools that generate from their training alone from tools that retrieve and cite documents, and explains why the latter still need checking
Explains why fluent, confident wording is not evidence of accuracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show an AI-generated paragraph on a topic the learner knows, containing a plausible but false statistic and a non-existent reference. Ask how such errors arise and which parts they would check first. Look for an explanation in terms of prediction from patterns rather than 'the AI lied' or 'its database had a mistake'.

topics.name: Interpreting AI policies
topics.description: Locate and interpret the rules on generative AI that apply to a specific task — institutional policy, programme and module guidance, the assessment brief and, for researchers, publisher and funder policies — including which kinds of use are permitted and what must be declared. Policies differ between and within institutions and change over time, so learners need a routine for checking each task and for asking when the rules are unclear.
masteryEvidence: Locates the AI rules for a given assessment and identifies the level or category of use permitted
Applies the rules to specific uses (grammar correction, translation, brainstorming, summarising readings, drafting) and identifies which are allowed
Recognises AI features embedded in everyday tools such as editors, translators and search engines as potentially covered by the policy
Writes a concise clarification request to a tutor when a use is not covered
Re-checks the rules for each module and assessment rather than assuming one rule applies everywhere
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a brief stating a mid-level permission (for example: AI may be used for planning and language feedback but not to generate assessed text, and all use must be declared) and five proposed uses. Ask the learner to classify each and say what would need declaring. Look for task-specific application and recognition of grey areas needing clarification.

topics.name: Acknowledging and citing AI use
topics.description: Declare and, where required, cite generative AI use in the form the institution, assessment or publisher specifies — typically stating which tools were used, for what purpose and at which stage, and keeping prompts and outputs as records — and distinguish acknowledging assistance from citing AI output as content. Transparent records also allow learners to demonstrate their own process if their work is questioned.
masteryEvidence: Writes a declaration stating tool, version or date, purpose, stage of use, and how outputs were evaluated or changed
Formats an in-text citation and reference for quoted or paraphrased AI output in the required style
Keeps a log of prompts, outputs and their own revisions and can produce it on request
Distinguishes uses that require declaration only, citation, or are not permitted
Applies publication norms that AI tools are not listed as authors and that their use is disclosed (PGR)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a declaration for an essay in which they used an AI tool to suggest counter-arguments to consider and to check grammar in the final draft. Check that it specifies tools, purposes, stages and their own evaluation, and is honest and proportionate rather than vague ('I used AI a bit').

topics.name: Verifying AI output
topics.description: Check AI output before relying on it: verify factual claims against authoritative sources, confirm that every reference exists and says what is attributed to it, check quotations and figures against the originals, and look for omissions and bias. Fabricated and erroneous citations are a documented failure of language models, so verification is a non-negotiable step whenever AI output informs academic work.
masteryEvidence: Checks each AI-supplied reference in a library database, publisher site or DOI resolver and identifies fabricated or altered ones
Traces key factual claims to an authoritative source using lateral reading
Compares an AI summary of a text with the text and identifies omissions, distortions and changes in certainty
Identifies missing perspectives or one-sided framing in AI output on a contested topic
Records what was verified, corrected and discarded
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an AI-generated paragraph with three references (one accurate, one real but misdescribed, one non-existent) and two factual claims, and allow ten minutes with library access. Strong performers find all reference problems through databases and check claims against sources rather than against another AI output.

topics.name: Using AI as a language-learning resource
topics.description: Use generative AI to support language development — explanations of grammar and vocabulary, feedback that identifies rather than silently fixes errors, practice dialogues and exercises, and comparison of alternative phrasings — in ways that keep the learner doing the cognitive work and stay within assessment rules. The aim is durable competence, so learners evaluate AI feedback critically and check whether their unassisted writing and speaking improve.
masteryEvidence: Requests feedback that locates and explains errors rather than a corrected version, then self-corrects
Evaluates AI language suggestions, identifying when a change alters meaning, certainty, register or disciplinary terminology
Uses AI to generate targeted practice on a recurring error and tests progress without the tool
Distinguishes the language support permitted for a task from rewriting that would breach its rules
Keeps a record of recurring error patterns identified through AI and other feedback
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to demonstrate how they would use an AI tool to improve a 100-word paragraph of their own for an assessment that permits language feedback but not rewriting. Check whether the prompts elicit explanation rather than replacement text, and whether the learner accepts, rejects or modifies suggestions with reasons.

topics.name: AI, authorship and voice
topics.description: Consider who is the author of a text produced with AI assistance — whose ideas, reasoning and words it contains, and who is accountable for them — and maintain one's own authorial voice and stance when using AI. AI-polished text can become generic and can misrepresent a writer's actual reasoning and competence, so learners decide where assistance must stop for a task to remain their own work. Where that line lies is contested: AI language polishing can also reduce the penalties multilingual writers face for non-standard English, much as proofreaders and literacy brokers do.
masteryEvidence: Explains why accountability for content, including errors, rests with the human author
Identifies changes to stance, hedging and positioning in an AI-edited version of their own paragraph
Revises an AI-edited passage to restore their own stance, claims and disciplinary positioning
Justifies a boundary for their own AI use in a task in terms of what the assessment is designed to show
Explains why AI tools are not credited as authors in scholarly publication
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner their own paragraph and an AI-'improved' version. Ask which they would submit, what changed in meaning, stance and voice, and which better represents their reasoning. Look for attention to claims, hedging and stance, not only to fluency.

topics.name: Limits of AI detection
topics.description: Understand that AI-text detectors estimate the likelihood that text was machine-generated, produce both false positives and false negatives, can be evaded, and have been shown to misclassify writing by people who use English as an additional language as AI-generated at high rates. Detector output therefore does not establish misconduct; institutions remain responsible for not treating such scores as evidence, and learners benefit from knowing their rights in integrity processes and from keeping ordinary records of their writing process (notes, drafts, version history), without being expected to prove their innocence.
masteryEvidence: Explains in plain terms why detectors that rely on measures of predictability can flag simple or formulaic human writing
Summarises evidence that detectors have misclassified writing by users of English as an additional language as AI-generated, and the limits of that evidence
Explains why a detector score alone cannot establish misconduct
Keeps evidence of their own writing process (notes, drafts, version history) for assessed work
Rejects 'humanising' or paraphrasing tools as a response to detectors and explains the integrity and quality risks
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask: 'A friend's essay was flagged as 80% AI-generated, but they wrote it themselves. What does the score mean, and what should they do?' Strong answers explain detector unreliability and bias, refer to the institution's process, and propose gathering drafts and version history rather than rewriting the essay to lower the score.

topics.name: Prompting for learning
topics.description: Write prompts that make AI act as a tutor or sparring partner — explanations at a chosen level, Socratic questions, worked examples followed by practice, counter-arguments, or feedback against criteria — rather than producing finished text, and judge whether the interaction produced learning. Effective prompting includes giving context and constraints, iterating, and stopping to work without the tool.
masteryEvidence: Writes prompts that specify role, level, task and constraints, such as asking to be questioned rather than given the answer
Uses AI to generate self-test questions or counter-arguments and answers them without assistance
Iterates a prompt when the output is too generic, too advanced or off-task
Judges whether an interaction increased their understanding by explaining the idea afterwards without the tool
Keeps prompting within the uses permitted for the task
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write two prompts for preparing a seminar on an assigned reading: one that would help them learn and one that would replace their thinking. Check the contrast (questioning, explanation and self-testing versus summary or answer generation) and whether the learning prompt includes constraints and a follow-up step done without the tool.

topics.name: AI-assisted research tools
topics.description: Evaluate and use AI-based literature discovery, question-answering and summarisation tools, understanding their limits in coverage, ranking, reproducibility and accuracy. These tools can speed up orientation to a field, but they cannot replace documented database searching, reading the sources themselves, or the researcher's own judgement of relevance and quality.
masteryEvidence: Compares results from an AI discovery tool with a structured database search on the same question and identifies differences in coverage
Checks AI-generated summaries of papers against the papers and identifies errors in findings, methods or certainty
Explains why AI tool searches are hard to reproduce and document, and records their use appropriately
Uses AI tools to find leads and then reads and cites the primary sources directly
Applies institutional and publisher rules on AI use in literature reviews
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to use an AI research tool on a narrow question in their field, then check the three most important papers it cites. Ask what the tool got right, what it misrepresented or missed, and how they would document its use. Look for checks against full texts rather than abstracts alone.

topics.name: Privacy, data and intellectual property with AI
topics.description: Judge what may and may not be entered into AI tools — personal and research-participant data, confidential or unpublished material, others' copyrighted work, and one's own unpublished work — taking account of the tool's terms on data retention and training, institutional data-protection rules and research ethics approvals. Learners also recognise that copyright in AI-generated content and in training data remains legally unsettled and varies by jurisdiction.
masteryEvidence: Identifies data in a coursework or research scenario that must not be uploaded to a public AI tool and explains why
Checks a tool's terms and institutional guidance on data retention and training use before uploading material
Explains how ethics approvals and consent forms constrain the use of AI tools with participant data
Explains why uploading copyrighted readings or others' unpublished manuscripts, for example when peer reviewing, may breach licences or confidentiality
Chooses institutionally approved tools or anonymisation where AI processing is permitted
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a scenario: a master's student wants to paste interview transcripts into a public chatbot to identify themes. Ask what must be checked first and what alternatives exist. Look for consent and ethics approval, data protection, the tool's data terms, anonymisation and approved tools.

topics.name: Values of academic integrity
topics.description: Explain the values that underpin academic integrity — honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage, as set out by the International Center for Academic Integrity — and connect them to everyday practices such as acknowledging sources, contributing fairly to group work and reporting data truthfully. A values framing presents integrity as a shared commitment of a scholarly community rather than only a set of prohibitions.
masteryEvidence: Names the six ICAI values and gives an academic practice that enacts each
Explains how a specific behaviour, such as sharing an answer file or inventing a data point, breaches particular values and who is affected
Relates integrity to the worth of their own qualification and to public trust in research
Reasons through an integrity dilemma by weighing competing values rather than citing a rule alone
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a short scenario (a friend asks to see your finished essay 'just for the structure') and ask the learner which values are at stake, what the risks are for each person, and what they would do. Look for reasoning from values and consequences, not only 'it is against the rules'.

topics.name: Understanding plagiarism
topics.description: Explain plagiarism as presenting others' words, ideas, data or work as one's own without adequate acknowledgement, and distinguish its forms: verbatim copying, patchwriting, missing or misleading citation, and borrowing structure or ideas. Learners should also understand why institutions weigh intention differently, why patchwriting is widely regarded as a developmental stage rather than deception, and that notions of textual ownership are historically and institutionally situated rather than universal.
masteryEvidence: Classifies examples of source use as acceptable, patchwriting, plagiarism of wording, plagiarism of ideas or structure, or citation error, and justifies each judgement
Explains why a citation does not make copied wording acceptable without quotation marks
Separates the textual question (what was borrowed and how it was signalled) from the question of intention, and states how their institution treats each
Explains, without stereotyping any group, why conventions of textual ownership vary across history and educational settings
Identifies practices in their own writing process, such as drafting with sources open or unmarked notes, that create risk
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give one source paragraph and four student versions: a correctly quoted and cited version, a close patchwrite with a citation, a good paraphrase with no citation, and a version that reuses the paragraph's line of argument in new words without citation. Ask the learner to rank and explain them. Check that both the cited patchwrite and the uncited paraphrase are recognised as problematic, for different reasons.

topics.name: Reusing one's own work
topics.description: Understand when and how one's own previous work may be reused. In coursework, most institutions treat resubmitting previously assessed work for credit as misconduct unless explicitly permitted; in research writing, reuse of text, data or findings (redundant or duplicate publication, text recycling) is governed by institutional, journal and publisher policies. Transparency — citing the earlier work, disclosing overlap and seeking permission where required — is the common principle.
masteryEvidence: Locates and explains the rule on reusing previously assessed work in their own programme regulations
Distinguishes legitimate development of earlier ideas, with self-citation and permission where needed, from resubmission for credit
Explains redundant publication and text recycling and why journals require disclosure of related submissions and publications
Cites their own earlier work, including dissertations, conference papers and preprints, where it is reused
Seeks advice from a tutor, supervisor or editor before reusing substantial material
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present three scenarios: reusing two paragraphs from a pre-sessional essay in a first-year assignment; developing a master's dissertation chapter into a journal article; submitting the same abstract to two conferences. Ask what the learner would need to check, disclose or cite in each. Look for reference to the specific policy and to transparency rather than a blanket yes or no.

topics.name: Collusion and legitimate collaboration
topics.description: Distinguish collusion — unauthorised collaboration on work assessed as individual, such as sharing drafts, answers or code, co-writing, or completing part of someone else's work — from legitimate collaboration such as discussing ideas, study groups, structured peer review and assessed group work. The boundary is set by each assessment's rules, so learners need to read the brief and ask when unsure.
masteryEvidence: Classifies collaborative behaviours for a given brief as permitted, permitted if acknowledged, or collusion
Explains the difference between discussing ideas and producing shared text, answers or code for individual submission
Identifies high-risk practices such as lending a finished file 'for reference' or a group dividing an individual task
Writes a clear, courteous refusal to a peer, or a clarification request to a tutor, when the boundary is unclear
Documents their own contribution to group work in the way the assessment requires
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an assessment brief and six scenarios (discussing the reading in a study group; comparing answers to an individual problem set before submission; peer reviewing a draft in class; sharing an essay plan; using a group's shared notes; lending a marked essay to a friend in the next cohort). Ask the learner to classify each and explain. Check that classifications are tied to the brief and to what is submitted as individual work.

topics.name: Contract cheating
topics.description: Recognise contract cheating — having a third party complete assessed work, whether paid or unpaid, through essay mills, 'tutoring' or 'editing' services that write content, file-exchange sites, friends or family — and the risks it carries, including detection, serious academic penalties, fraud, loss of personal data and blackmail by providers. Knowing how providers market themselves helps learners resist offers when under pressure.
masteryEvidence: Defines contract cheating and gives examples beyond paid essay mills, including unpaid help from friends and 'editing' that rewrites content
Identifies common marketing claims (model answers, plagiarism-free guarantees, native-speaker writers) and explains why they are misleading
Explains the academic, legal, financial and personal risks, including blackmail and misuse of personal data
Distinguishes permitted support (writing centres, permitted proofreading, tutors explaining concepts) from outsourcing
Names the institutional support routes to use instead
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a constructed social-media message offering 'custom model essays, 100% plagiarism-free, written by native speakers' and ask the learner what is being offered, what the risks are, and what legitimate alternatives exist. Look for recognition that submitting a 'model' essay is outsourced work, awareness of blackmail and data risks, and named alternatives.

topics.name: Interpreting similarity reports
topics.description: Read a text-matching (similarity) report critically: it shows overlaps between a submission and indexed material, not plagiarism; matches must be interpreted by type (quoted and cited text, reference entries, common phrases, patchwriting, unattributed copying); and, where permitted, reports can be used formatively to improve source use. An overall percentage has no fixed meaning, and whether misconduct has occurred is decided by people applying policy, not by software.
masteryEvidence: Explains what text-matching software compares a submission with and what it cannot detect, such as paraphrased ideas, translated or outsourced work and unindexed sources
Classifies highlighted matches in a sample report as acceptable or needing revision and explains why
Explains why a high overall percentage can be acceptable and a low one can coexist with plagiarism
Revises a patchwritten passage flagged in a formative report by rewriting from understanding of the source, not by synonym substitution
States that institutional processes, not the score, determine whether misconduct has occurred
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a sample report with a 28% overall score in which most matches are cited quotations and reference-list entries, plus one uncited 40-word patchwritten passage. Ask whether there is a problem and what the writer should do. Strong answers disregard the headline figure, locate the patchwritten passage and propose rewriting it from understanding with a citation.

topics.name: Integrity policies and processes
topics.description: Locate and interpret the integrity regulations that apply: definitions of misconduct, module-level rules, procedures for suspected cases, possible outcomes, and rights to support, representation and appeal. Knowing the process reduces fear, helps learners respond appropriately and in time if concerns are raised, and makes clear that policies and terminology vary between institutions and modules. Learners should also know their procedural rights: to see the evidence, to respond in a language and format they can use (including interpreting or language support where offered), to be accompanied, and to have indicators such as similarity scores, AI-detector output or differences in writing style weighed by people alongside their own account.
masteryEvidence: Finds the institution's integrity policy and the module-level rules for a given assessment
Summarises the stages of their institution's process for a suspected case, including who decides and on what evidence
Identifies sources of independent advice and support, such as a students' union advice service, and when to contact them
Drafts a factual, appropriately formal reply to an invitation to an integrity meeting, including evidence of their writing process
Explains the grounds for appeal as their institution defines them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a constructed letter inviting a student to an integrity meeting about an essay. Ask: what is being alleged, what should the student do in the next 48 hours, what evidence of their writing process could they bring, and who can support them? Check use of the actual policy and support services, and a measured response that is neither panicked nor dismissive.

topics.name: Managing integrity risk under pressure
topics.description: Recognise the conditions under which shortcuts become tempting — clustered deadlines, illness, financial or visa-related pressure, low confidence in English, unclear tasks — and act early: plan workload, request extensions or submit extenuating-circumstances claims through proper channels, use academic and wellbeing support, and ask for clarification rather than guessing or outsourcing.
masteryEvidence: Identifies early-warning signs of integrity risk in their own workload and wellbeing
Explains their institution's extension and extenuating-circumstances procedures and deadlines
Writes an appropriate extension or clarification request
Uses at least one academic support service before a deadline crisis
Chooses a lower-risk option (partial or late submission, extension request) over a shortcut in a dilemma scenario and explains why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a scenario: three deadlines in one week, a family emergency, and a friend offering to 'help write' one essay. Ask the learner to plan the next 72 hours. Look for use of formal procedures and support services, prioritisation, and a reasoned refusal of the offer.

topics.name: Research integrity
topics.description: Understand the standards of responsible research: honesty in proposing, conducting and reporting research; the avoidance of fabrication, falsification and plagiarism; questionable research practices such as selective reporting, undisclosed changes to hypotheses or analyses and inappropriate authorship; and data management that makes research verifiable. Research students apply these standards to their own data, records, theses and publications.
masteryEvidence: Defines fabrication, falsification and plagiarism and gives an example of each from their own field
Identifies questionable research practices in case scenarios and explains how they distort the research record
Describes how they record, store and version data and analyses so that results can be checked
Reports methods, exclusions and departures from plans transparently in a project report or thesis
Identifies the institutional, funder and journal codes of conduct that apply to their research
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short case: a master's student excludes three 'outlier' participants after seeing that this makes the result significant and does not mention it in the dissertation. Ask what is problematic, what should have been done and how it should be reported. Look for recognition of undisclosed analytic flexibility and transparent alternatives, such as pre-specified exclusion criteria or reporting both analyses.

dependencies.reason: Deciding what needs citing applies the purposes of citation (credit and verifiability) to specific pieces of content
Common knowledge is defined relative to a discourse community, so learners need that concept to judge what their readers already share
Systems are easier to compare and remember once learners see them as different solutions to the same needs for credit and retrievability
Learners must identify which author–date variant their guide prescribes before they can format citations in it
Formatting and placing citations presupposes knowing which content in a text needs to be cited
et al. and similar abbreviations recur in author–date citations and are frequently misused or mispunctuated
Numeric formatting rules make sense only once learners know that sequence-based systems differ in principle from author–date systems
Numbering citations presupposes knowing which content needs to be cited
Entry format and list order depend on which system and guide apply
Entries are built by source type, so learners must first recognise whether an item is an article, a chapter, a report or a web page
Guides require sentence case for some title elements and title case for others, and this is one of the most frequent reference-list errors
Full notes and bibliography entries are built from the same bibliographic elements as reference-list entries
Placing notes requires knowing which content needs citing and keeping citation separate from discursive commentary
Citing an unfamiliar source type means adapting the known core elements (who, when, what, where) of reference entries
Recognising grey literature, preprints, datasets and versions depends on knowing how such outputs are produced and published
Locators are obligatory with direct quotation, so learners must first know what counts as quoting and when to quote
Checking details requires knowing which elements an entry must contain and how they are formatted
Cross-checking citations against entries depends on control of in-text forms, which in most EAP settings are author–date
Much checking in practice means correcting reference-manager output, which is easier when learners know how the tool generates entries from item metadata
Proofreading techniques such as separate passes and checklists transfer directly to systematic citation checking
The detailed typology of citation functions refines a basic understanding of what sources do in a writer's text
Functions are realised partly through the choice of integral or non-integral form
Evaluative and comparative functions are often signalled by the evaluative force of reporting verbs
Comparing disciplines requires an analytical vocabulary for citation forms and functions
Explaining citation differences draws on how disciplines differ in what counts as knowledge and how it accumulates
Knowing what counts as generative AI, including features embedded in other tools, is needed to see which uses a policy covers
Grey areas in AI policies are easier to resolve when the rules are understood as protecting honesty and fairness
AI rules are usually stated per assessment, so reading them is part of analysing the assignment brief
Understanding what an assessment is designed to evidence explains why permitted AI use differs between tasks
What must be declared or cited, and in what form, is set by the applicable policy
Citing AI output applies the general procedure for non-standard and non-recoverable source types
Knowing why models fabricate and distort tells learners what to check and why fluency is no guarantee
Checking claims against independent sources is the core verification move for factual content
Confirming that references exist requires searching library databases, discovery tools or DOI records
Recognising altered or fabricated references depends on knowing which bibliographic elements to check
Designing prompts that elicit useful explanation and questions depends on understanding how models respond to context and instructions
Learners need to know which interactions are permitted for a task before using AI to prepare for it
Using AI for learning requires setting goals, monitoring understanding and evaluating outcomes, the phases of self-regulated learning
Using AI to build language competence depends on prompting for explanation and feedback rather than replacement text
Learners make better use of AI feedback when they already know how to process and act on written corrective feedback
Judging how AI assistance affects voice requires a concept of authorial voice and stance
Questions of AI authorship extend the principle that submitted work must not misrepresent whose words and ideas it contains
Understanding prediction-based generation helps explain why AI-edited text tends towards generic phrasing and stance
Why detectors misfire, including on predictable human writing, can only be explained with a basic model of how text is generated
The principle that software output is an indicator requiring human judgement, not a verdict, is first established with similarity reports
AI research tools are useful only if their citations and summaries are verified against the sources
Judging an AI summary requires knowing what an accurate summary of the whole text would contain
Evaluating AI discovery output depends on knowing what a map of the relevant literature should include
Privacy risks follow from how inputs may be stored, processed and used for training
Knowing how copyright and licences govern access to and reuse of published work underpins judgements about uploading texts
Obligations around participant data, confidentiality and data management come from research integrity and ethics
Plagiarism is defined by a failure of acknowledgement, so learners must first understand what citation does and for whom
The values frame plagiarism as a breach of honesty and fairness rather than a technical rule, which supports judgement in unclear cases
Rules on self-reuse extend the plagiarism concept of misrepresentation to one's own earlier work
Resubmission is misconduct because each assessment is meant to evidence new learning against its outcomes
Collusion is best explained through fairness to other students and honesty about whose work is being assessed
Knowing why universities value collaboration prevents learners from overcorrecting into avoiding all legitimate peer learning
Contract cheating is a form of misrepresented authorship, and the plagiarism concept supplies that core idea
Interpreting matches requires knowing which kinds of borrowing are acceptable and which are not
Many highlighted matches are patchwriting, which learners must recognise and know how to revise from understanding
Understanding an allegation requires knowing the forms of misconduct the policy defines
Similarity reports often prompt concerns, so knowing their limited evidential status helps learners respond appropriately
Regulations rely on institutional vocabulary (assessment board, extenuating circumstances, appeal) that learners must understand to follow the process
The strategy consists of turning to support services and formal procedures, which learners must know exist and how to access
Learners need to recognise outsourcing offers as a risk before they can plan to resist them under pressure
Many integrity crises begin as workload crises that planning and prioritising can prevent
Extension and clarification requests are the main legitimate alternatives to shortcuts and require appropriately mitigated requests
Plagiarism is one of the three core forms of research misconduct alongside fabrication and falsification
Why fabrication and selective reporting matter depends on understanding how research enters, and is relied on in, the scholarly record

guidance.summary: Learners often meet citation first as a plagiarism-avoidance rule, which encourages mechanical or defensive citing. Teaching can start instead from what citation does for readers and writers: Hyland (1999) shows citation as central to how disciplines construct knowledge and how writers align themselves with a community, and Swales (1986) argued for reading citations as discourse rather than simply counting them. Pecorari (2013) recommends making the communicative rationale explicit before the mechanics, so that later decisions have a principle behind them.

activities.title: What does this citation do?
learnerActions: Read a short expert or exemplar paragraph with its citations highlighted
For each citation, note what a reader could check or follow up because of it and whose work is credited
Reread the paragraph with the citations removed, as a sceptical marker, and mark claims that now look unsupported or appear to be the writer's own
Agree a class list of citation purposes to reuse in later units
activities.intendedInsight: Citations make claims checkable, give credit, and show the writer knows the field; without them the writer silently claims others' work and loses credibility.
activities.rationale: Moving from a rule to purposes gives learners a principle they can apply to new cases. Hyland's account of citation as knowledge construction supports this framing, and Bretag et al.'s survey, in which students asked to be taught how to do it properly, supports explicit, purpose-led teaching.

activities.title: Following a claim through the conversation
learnerActions: Take one cited claim from a recent article and find the cited source
Note what the original actually said and how the citing author used it (agreeing, extending, criticising)
Draw a simple chain showing how the claim travelled across two or three texts
Discuss what a reader could not do if the chain were broken
activities.intendedInsight: Citations link texts into a conversation that readers can enter and check; a writer's citations are a public trail others will follow.
activities.rationale: Gives concrete experience of the ACRL frame 'Scholarship as Conversation' and of verifiability, and prepares learners for later work on citation accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: 'I cite so that I don't get caught for plagiarism.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations appear only beside quotations or are added after drafting to 'cover' the text; the learner cannot say what a citation tells the reader.
difficulties.response: Reframe citation around reader needs (checking, following up, credit) with model texts. Avoid fear-based framing that equates citation with compliance, which tends to produce defensive over-citation and anxiety.

difficulties.pattern: 'Citing other people makes my work look less original.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Few citations in argumentative writing; authoritative-sounding claims left unattributed; reading presented as the writer's own knowledge.
difficulties.response: Show how expert writers make their own contribution visible against cited work; ask learners to mark which claims in an exemplar are the writer's own and how citation makes them stand out. Present this as a community expectation to be made explicit, not as a learner deficiency.

difficulties.pattern: 'Textbooks and lectures don't cite much, so I don't need to cite them either.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Ideas, figures or diagrams from lecture slides and textbooks reproduced without attribution.
difficulties.response: Contrast genres: textbooks and lectures consolidate knowledge for learners and often cite lightly, whereas assessed writing must display its sources. Show how to cite lecture material where the department permits it, or how to trace it to the original source.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Give me three reasons why academic writers cite sources, other than avoiding plagiarism, with an example of each.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives three or more distinct purposes (credit, verifiability, joining or positioning within a debate, supporting a claim, credibility with the reader) with apt examples.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives credit and support for claims but cannot explain verifiability or positioning, or lists purposes without examples.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Mentions only avoiding plagiarism or penalties, or describes citation as a formality.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, keep to credit, evidence and checking, using textbooks and short articles. On pre-sessional courses, connect the purposes directly to the source-based assignment and its marking criteria. In UG in-sessional work, link to the student's discipline as a bridge to rhetorical functions and disciplinary variation.

guidance.summary: Common knowledge is the hardest boundary in citation because it depends on reader, discipline and level. Shi (2011) found that students and their instructors did not always agree about what needed citing and that students' judgements were bound up with what they had themselves just learned. Teaching should therefore build a decision procedure and practise borderline cases rather than offer a fixed list. Pecorari (2013) also stresses that ideas, data and argument structure need attribution, not only wording — a gap that appears when citation is taught mainly alongside quotation.

activities.title: Cite, don't cite, it depends
learnerActions: In pairs, sort twelve statement cards from a recently studied topic into 'cite', 'no need' and 'depends'
For each 'depends' card, write the condition that would decide it (readership, discipline, how specific or contested the claim is)
Compare with another pair and with the tutor's sorting, discussing disagreements rather than seeking a single answer
Write a personal rule of thumb for doubtful cases
activities.intendedInsight: Common knowledge is a judgement about a particular readership; specific figures, findings, frameworks and contested claims almost always need a source.
activities.rationale: Because judgements of common knowledge vary even among experienced academics, discussing borderline cases and the criteria behind them is likely to transfer better than memorising a list.

activities.title: Hidden borrowing audit
learnerActions: Highlight every idea, figure, example or line of argument in a paragraph of their own draft that came from reading or lectures
Check each highlighted item for a citation
Add missing citations or reformulate to separate their own reasoning from source content
Note which kinds of borrowing (data, examples, argument structure) they most often left uncited
activities.intendedInsight: Ideas, data and the organisation of an argument need attribution as well as copied words.
activities.rationale: Self-audit applies the criteria to the learner's own text, where the hardest decisions occur, and builds self-monitoring rather than reliance on text-matching software.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I change the words, I don't need to cite.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Competently paraphrased content with no citation; surprise when told an idea needs attribution.
difficulties.response: Contrast attribution of ideas with attribution of wording using a side-by-side example: paraphrase changes the wording, not the ownership. Return to the purposes of citation.

difficulties.pattern: 'It's on lots of websites, so it's common knowledge.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncited statistics, definitions or named theories justified because they are widely available online.
difficulties.response: Distinguish 'widely available' from 'known to the intended readers without looking it up'. Use the reader-oriented question: would my marker ask where this comes from?

difficulties.pattern: Every sentence ends in a citation, including the writer's own conclusions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citations attached to evaluative or concluding sentences that are the writer's own inference, so the writer's contribution disappears.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a cautious stage, not an error to penalise. Ask the learner to mark which sentences are their own inference and to remove citations that wrongly attribute them. Do not simply say 'cite less' without showing what remains theirs.

diagnostic.task: Give five statements (a specific statistic, a historical date taught in most schools, a named theory and its core claim, a contested causal claim, and the learner's own inference from two sources) and ask which need citing and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Cites the statistic, the theory and the contested claim; treats the date as probably common knowledge for this readership; does not cite the inference but signals it as their own; reasons refer to reader and specificity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but reasons are rule-based ('statistics need citations') or the learner is unsure how to treat the inference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would cite only items that are quoted, or would cite nothing that has been paraphrased.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need concrete categories (numbers, findings, definitions, images) and a 'cite if in doubt' default. Pre-sessional learners apply the procedure across an extended project, where uncited reading-derived ideas are a common concern. UG and PGT in-sessional work should address disciplinary common knowledge — what specialist readers take for granted — and over-citation of the writer's own synthesis.
reviewNotes: shi2011 is a proposed reference; if it cannot be verified, the claim about disagreement over common knowledge needs another source or must be softened.

guidance.summary: Learners often arrive believing there is one correct way to reference. Teaching should present the families of systems and what each foregrounds — author and date (APA 7; Chicago author–date), MLA 9's author and page, sequence (IEEE; the NLM-based Vancouver style recommended through the ICMJE Recommendations), or notes with pinpoints (Chicago notes and bibliography; OSCOLA) — and train learners to find and follow the authoritative guide for each context. 'Harvard' has no single authority: it is a family of institution-specific variants, so learners should always check which version their department prescribes.

activities.title: System spotting
learnerActions: Examine five short extracts with reference lists or notes from different disciplines
Identify each system family from the in-text form and list order
Find the official or departmental guide that governs two of them
Note one design feature of each system and what it makes easy for the reader
activities.intendedInsight: Different systems meet the same needs differently, and the governing guide decides the details.
activities.rationale: Contrasting authentic texts builds recognition and the habit of consulting the authority; linking design to reader needs reduces the sense that styles are arbitrary.

activities.title: Which Harvard?
learnerActions: Compare two universities' Harvard guides for the same three sources
List the differences in punctuation, capitalisation and element order
Identify and bookmark the version that applies to their own course
Select or adjust a reference-manager output style and check that it matches that version
activities.intendedInsight: There is no single Harvard, so consistency with the specified version matters more than memorising one model.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses the belief that Harvard is a fixed standard and turns variation into a practical checking routine.

difficulties.pattern: 'My previous school taught me the right way to reference, so this department's style is wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Formats from a previous institution persist after explicit instruction; resistance to departmental guidance.
difficulties.response: Validate prior learning as a legitimate convention, then frame the task as switching systems on demand, as researchers do between journals. Provide a side-by-side comparison of the old and new styles.

difficulties.pattern: 'APA and Harvard are the same thing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: APA-specific rules used where an institutional Harvard is specified, or vice versa, producing a mixed style.
difficulties.response: Show the specific points where the two prescribed guides diverge and stress checking the brief. Do not overstate the stakes: markers mainly notice inconsistency and missing information.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your module handbook says use Harvard. Where do you find the rules, and what would you do if your reference manager's Harvard output differs from them?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the departmental or library guide as the authority, notes that Harvard varies, and would select or edit the manager's output style to match the guide.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows a guide is needed but assumes any Harvard guide or the software default will do.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Believes there is one universal Harvard or treats it as interchangeable with any author–date style.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses usually teach one author–date style but should name the others so learners recognise them in reading. UG and PGT in-sessional sessions focus on the department's prescribed style, including numeric styles in engineering and medicine and OSCOLA in law. PGR writers switch between journal styles and should treat each journal's author guidelines as the authority.
reviewNotes: Style guides are revised periodically (for example Chicago's 18th edition appeared in 2024); confirm which edition institutions currently prescribe.

guidance.summary: Author–date citation is usually the first system taught in EAP because most general EAP programmes use APA 7 or an institutional Harvard. Linking formatting to the integral/non-integral distinction (Swales, 1990; Thompson & Tribble, 2001) gives the mechanics a rhetorical rationale and is likely to be more useful than an isolated rule list, although this has not been tested, and when learners practise placing citations so that the scope of attribution is clear. Learners should consult the guide for edge cases rather than memorise them; the stable core is who, when and, for quotations, where.

activities.title: Narrative or parenthetical?
learnerActions: Find six citations in a model text and sort them into narrative (author named in the sentence) and parenthetical forms
Rewrite two narrative citations as parenthetical and two parenthetical as narrative, adjusting sentence grammar
Discuss how each change shifts emphasis between the author and the information
Apply the guide's rules for two-author and three-or-more-author works to the rewritten citations
activities.intendedInsight: Format follows grammatical role, and the choice of form changes what the sentence foregrounds.
activities.rationale: Linking mechanics to the integral/non-integral distinction gives form a function and prepares learners for later rhetorical choices.

activities.title: Citation clinic and personal checklist
learnerActions: Correct ten citations containing typical errors (given names, missing year, et al. misuse, ampersand in narrative form, unordered multiple works)
Check each correction against the specified guide and record the rule
Write a checklist of the three errors they personally make most often
Apply the checklist to their current draft
activities.intendedInsight: A few recurring errors account for most citation problems, and these can be self-checked.
activities.rationale: Targeted error work with a self-made checklist builds monitoring of one's own recurring patterns rather than dependence on teacher correction.

difficulties.pattern: Citing with given names, initials or full names ('John Smith (2020)'), or citing the wrong part of a name.
difficulties.revealedBy: Given or full names in citations; author names differing between citation and reference list; compound or particle surnames split wrongly.
difficulties.response: In naming systems where the family name comes first, or where given names are the usual form of reference, learners may be unsure which name to cite. Teach the guide's surname-only rule and show how to identify the family name from the article's metadata or the author's other publications.

difficulties.pattern: One citation placed at the end of a long paragraph that mixes source content and the writer's comments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers cannot tell which sentences are attributed; markers comment that the writer's own view is unclear.
difficulties.response: Show how to mark where attributed content starts (a narrative citation or signal phrase) and ends, re-citing where necessary. Avoid insisting on a citation after every sentence, which hides the writer's own contribution.

difficulties.pattern: 'et al. means and others, so I can use it for two authors.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'et al.' for two-author works, mispunctuated forms such as 'et. al', or 'et al.' in reference-list entries.
difficulties.response: Contrast the guide's rule for two authors with three or more, and note that reference lists normally give authors in full up to the guide's limit.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite a two-author source narratively, a five-author source parenthetically, and both sources together in one parenthesis.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All forms correct for the guide, including 'and' versus '&', et al. for the five-author source and correct ordering of the two works.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Basic forms correct but errors in ordering multiple works or in the two-author narrative form.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses given names, omits years, or applies et al. to the two-author source.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, teach the core forms with books and journal articles. Pre-sessional courses should add group authors, multiple works and secondary citation, which appear in extended projects. UG and PGT in-sessional sessions can focus on the department's variant and on citation placement within synthesis paragraphs.

guidance.summary: Numeric systems are often neglected on general EAP courses that teach only author–date, leaving engineering, computing and health students to learn them unaided. The mechanics are simple but the rhetoric differs: numbers background cited authors, consistent with Hyland's (1999) finding that the hard sciences in his corpus favoured non-integral citation, so naming an author becomes a marked choice. Teaching should combine the authoritative guide (the IEEE Reference Guide; for Vancouver, the NLM-based style recommended in the ICMJE Recommendations or the journal's own instructions) with practice in reference-manager numbering.

activities.title: Renumber after revision
learnerActions: Move one paragraph earlier in a short IEEE-style text
Renumber all citations in order of first appearance and reorder the reference list by hand
Repeat the task using a reference manager and compare time and accuracy
Note which errors the software prevents and which it cannot, such as wrong item metadata
activities.intendedInsight: Numeric systems depend on sequence, which is fragile under revision; software helps with sequence but metadata still needs checking.
activities.rationale: Simulates the main practical difficulty of numeric styles and motivates disciplined reference-manager use.

activities.title: When to name the author
learnerActions: Highlight every sentence in an engineering or medical article where an author is named alongside a citation number
Classify why the author is named (contrast between studies, credit for a method, critique)
Rewrite two non-integral citations so that the author is named and judge whether the change is justified
Agree a rule of thumb for naming authors in numeric systems
activities.intendedInsight: In numeric systems, naming an author is a marked choice used for emphasis, contrast or evaluation.
activities.rationale: Connects formatting to Hyland's observation that disciplines differ in how prominently cited authors appear.

difficulties.pattern: Numbering sources alphabetically or in the order they appear in the reference-manager library.
difficulties.revealedBy: Alphabetised reference list; citation numbers that do not ascend through the text.
difficulties.response: Restate the principle of order of first citation and give a short renumbering exercise.

difficulties.pattern: Giving a repeated source a new number each time it is cited.
difficulties.revealedBy: Duplicate entries in the reference list under different numbers.
difficulties.response: Show that a number identifies a source, not an occurrence; merge duplicates in the reference manager.

difficulties.pattern: 'Numeric styles don't use page numbers', so quotations carry only the citation number.
difficulties.revealedBy: Direct quotations with no locator.
difficulties.response: Show how the specified style adds a page or section to the citation when quoting, and note that direct quotation is itself uncommon in these fields.

diagnostic.task: Give three sources cited in the order B, A, B, C and ask the learner to write the in-text numbers and the reference-list order in IEEE style.
diagnostic.strongResponse: B is [1], A is [2], B again is [1], C is [3]; list ordered B, A, C with entries in IEEE format.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sequence correct but B given a new number on repetition, or entries not in IEEE format.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Alphabetical numbering, or author–date elements mixed in.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation pathways into engineering, computing or medicine, introduce numeric citation alongside author–date so learners recognise both. Pre-sessional courses with discipline-specific strands should assess the style students will meet. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, follow the department's variant; PGR writers switch between journal-specific numeric styles.
reviewNotes: Vancouver is a family of numeric styles derived from NLM's Citing Medicine and adapted by journals; the journal's instructions are usually the operative authority.

guidance.summary: Note-based systems serve fields in which pinpointing, discursive commentary and varied primary sources matter, such as history, much of the humanities and law. Chicago (18th ed.) sets out full notes, shortened notes and bibliography; OSCOLA governs much UK legal writing, where cases and legislation have their own formats and pinpoints are expected. Teaching should separate the citation function of notes from their discursive use, which learners tend either to overuse or to avoid.

activities.title: From full note to short note to bibliography
