learnerActions: Write a full first note for a book and a journal article in the specified guide
Write shortened notes for later citations of the same works with different pages
Compile the bibliography entries and compare punctuation and name order with the notes
Check the guide's current rule for consecutive citations of the same source
activities.intendedInsight: Notes and bibliography entries share elements but differ in punctuation and name order, and shortened notes depend on a full first note.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison of note and bibliography forms targets the most frequent formatting confusions.

activities.title: Primary and secondary authorities (law)
learnerActions: Sort a list of authorities into primary (cases, legislation) and secondary (books, articles)
Format two cases and one statute with pinpoints in OSCOLA
Add a footnote citing a journal article with a pinpoint page
Check whether the module requires tables of cases and legislation
activities.intendedInsight: Legal citation distinguishes primary authorities from commentary and expects precise pinpoints.
activities.rationale: OSCOLA formats for primary legal sources are unfamiliar to most learners and central to legal writing assessment.

difficulties.pattern: Long explanations that belong in the argument are placed in footnotes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Key argument steps or definitions appear only in notes; the main text reads as thin.
difficulties.response: Agree a test: if the reader needs it to follow the argument, it belongs in the main text. Show expert examples of short discursive notes.

difficulties.pattern: Author–date parenthetical citations mixed into a notes system.
difficulties.revealedBy: (Author, Year) in the text alongside footnotes.
difficulties.response: Explain that the systems are alternatives, then convert one paragraph fully to notes.

difficulties.pattern: Note numbers placed inconsistently or typed manually as superscripts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Numbers before and after punctuation in the same text; notes that do not renumber after editing.
difficulties.response: Point to the guide's placement rule and use the word processor's footnote function or a reference manager.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite the same book twice in footnotes (pages 12 and 40) and give its bibliography entry in the specified guide.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Full note then shortened note with correct pinpoints; bibliography entry with inverted name and the guide's punctuation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Repeats the full note, omits pinpoints, or copies the note format into the bibliography.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses parenthetical author–date citations or gives no locators.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses with law or humanities pathways should introduce notes before progression. In UG and PGT in-sessional teaching the department's guide is the authority; PGR writers in history and law also need control of archival, legal and non-English sources in notes.
reviewNotes: OSCOLA (5th ed., 2026) and Chicago (18th ed., 2024) have both been revised recently; departments may still prescribe earlier editions during transition, so confirm the edition specified.

guidance.summary: Reference-list accuracy depends less on memorising models than on identifying the source type and locating its elements in the source, a step learners skip when they copy citations from search results. APA 7, MLA 9 and Chicago all organise entries around a small set of elements (author, date, title, source or container), and MLA 9 makes this core-element logic explicit, so teaching the elements first makes new formats easier to construct. Reference managers reduce workload but generate predictable errors that learners must be trained to check.

activities.title: Element hunt
learnerActions: Label the author(s), date, title, container, editors, publisher, volume and issue, pages and DOI on a PDF article, a book's title and copyright pages, and a chapter in an edited book
Classify each source type
Build the reference entries from the labelled elements
Check the entries against the guide and a classmate's version
activities.intendedInsight: Entries are assembled from elements located in the source, and the source type decides which elements are needed and in what order.
activities.rationale: Element-first teaching is likely to transfer better to unfamiliar source types than copying model entries.

activities.title: Exported reference audit
learnerActions: Export references for five sources from a library database or reference manager
Compare each with the guide and highlight errors in capitalisation, item type, names and missing elements
Correct the entries and note which errors recur
Fix the item type or metadata fields in the reference manager so the error does not recur
activities.intendedInsight: Automatically generated references are drafts that need checking.
activities.rationale: Mirrors real practice and prepares learners for systematic accuracy checks.

difficulties.pattern: A chapter in an edited book is referenced as if it were the whole book.
difficulties.revealedBy: Chapter author given as book author; editors missing; no chapter page range.
difficulties.response: Use the title and contents pages to show the two levels of authorship and the idea of a container.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll list everything I read, including sources I didn't cite.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference list longer than the set of in-text citations.
difficulties.response: Distinguish a reference list from a bibliography and check which the brief requires.

difficulties.pattern: Capitalising every main word of article and book titles in APA.
difficulties.revealedBy: Title case for article and book titles in an APA reference list, often carried over from the source's own display or from another style.
difficulties.response: Teach sentence case versus title case explicitly in context, with proper nouns as the exception, and show where the guide requires each.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a PDF of a journal article and ask for its reference entry in the specified style within three minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All elements present and correct, including the DOI in the required form, title capitalisation, and italics for journal name and volume where required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Elements present but with formatting errors in capitalisation, italics or DOI form.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Missing elements, wrong author order, or the URL of a search page instead of a DOI.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners should control books, journal articles and web pages. Pre-sessional courses add chapters in edited books, reports and checking of reference-manager output. UG and PGT in-sessional work extends to the department's style and the source types common in the discipline.

guidance.summary: As assignments draw on reports, datasets, software, media and AI tools, learners increasingly meet sources with no exact model in their guide. The transferable skill is to identify who is responsible, which version, when, and how a reader can retrieve it, then adapt the closest model; APA 7 and MLA 9 both encourage this reasoning. Practice should include sources the reader cannot retrieve, such as personal communications and most AI conversations, whose treatment differs between guides and institutions.

activities.title: No-model challenge
learnerActions: In groups, receive three unusual sources such as an NGO report, a dataset and a podcast episode
Identify the author, date, title, version and retrieval information for each
Find the closest model in the guide and adapt it
Explain the reasoning to the class and compare with the guide's examples or library advice
activities.intendedInsight: Citing unfamiliar sources is reasoning from elements, not finding an exact template.
activities.rationale: Builds transferable reasoning for the long tail of source types that no guide fully covers.

activities.title: Citing AI output
learnerActions: Read the current guidance for AI output from the specified style guide and the module's AI policy
Note whether the guide treats the tool or its developer as author, how the prompt is described, and whether a reference-list entry is needed
Cite a short AI output as the guide requires and write the accompanying description of its use
Compare two guides' advice and discuss why they differ
activities.intendedInsight: Guidance on AI output is recent, varies between guides and institutions, and is usually combined with a declaration of use.
activities.rationale: AI outputs are typically non-recoverable for readers, which makes them an instructive limit case; because guidance is evolving, learners need the habit of checking the current version.

difficulties.pattern: 'There's no author, so I'll write Anonymous or the website name.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Anonymous' or a domain name given as author for organisational web pages and reports.
difficulties.response: Show that organisations can be authors, and how the guide treats genuinely authorless items.

difficulties.pattern: 'Datasets and software aren't texts, so they don't need citing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Data sources and analysis software named in a methods section without citation or version.
difficulties.response: Connect to the purposes of citation: credit for data creators and reproducibility of the analysis.

difficulties.pattern: Treating an AI tool as an author whose views can be attributed ('ChatGPT argues that…').
difficulties.revealedBy: AI tools in narrative citations as if they were scholarly authorities.
difficulties.response: Explain that AI output is generated text, not an authored, accountable source; follow the guide's format for documenting use and verify any substantive claim against a scholarly source.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite an organisational report on a website, a dataset with a version number, and a lecture recording at a specific minute.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Organisation as author; dataset version and identifier included; timestamp given; formats adapted correctly from the guide.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One or two items correct; uses 'Anonymous' or omits version or timestamp.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify the elements, or gives the URL alone.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should focus on web pages, reports and lecture materials. UG and PGT in-sessional work extends to datasets, software, standards and media relevant to the discipline. PGR writers need data and software citation for reproducibility and may need to follow journal or funder data policies.
reviewNotes: Guidance on citing generative AI output is evolving and differs between style guides; check current guidance before teaching. mcadoo2023 is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Locators are a small skill with a large effect on verifiability and on markers' judgements of care. Guides agree that quotations need a locator but differ on paraphrase: APA 7 encourages page or paragraph numbers for paraphrases, particularly of specific passages in long works; MLA 9 builds the page number into the citation; and Chicago notes and OSCOLA expect pinpoints. Teaching should cover sources without page numbers, where learners most often omit locators altogether.

activities.title: Locator ladder
learnerActions: Quote from a paginated book, an unpaginated web article, a video and a long report with numbered sections
Choose the appropriate locator for each (page, paragraph, heading, timestamp, section)
Format each in the specified guide
Swap with a partner and test whether the quotation can be found in under a minute
activities.intendedInsight: A locator should let a reader find the material quickly, whatever the medium.
activities.rationale: A reader-oriented test is easier to apply to new cases than recalled rules.

activities.title: Pinpoint the paraphrase
learnerActions: Paraphrase one specific argument from a long chapter
Decide whether to add a page number and justify the decision
Compare the decision with the guide's recommendation
Revise the citation if needed
activities.intendedInsight: Locators for paraphrase help readers verify specific claims drawn from long works.
activities.rationale: Targets the rule that varies most between guides.

difficulties.pattern: 'Web pages have no page numbers, so no locator is needed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Quotations from online sources and videos without any locator.
difficulties.response: Teach paragraph numbers, headings and timestamps as alternative locators.

difficulties.pattern: Page numbers taken from the PDF viewer rather than the printed pagination.
difficulties.revealedBy: Locators such as 'p. 3' for an article printed as pages 345–367.
difficulties.response: Show the difference between viewer pages and journal pagination; use the printed page numbers.

difficulties.pattern: Quotation marks used but the locator forgotten, especially when quoting short phrases.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent locators within one text; locators present for long quotations only.
difficulties.response: Add a locator check to the learner's personal citation checklist; do not re-teach the whole rule if the learner can state it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to cite a quotation from page 3 of a PDF of a journal article whose printed pages are 112–130, and a quotation from a 20-minute online video.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses the printed page (for example p. 114) and a timestamp, both in the guide's format.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One locator correct; uses the PDF page or omits the timestamp.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No locators.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation: quotations with page numbers from books and articles. Pre-sessional: unpaginated and audiovisual sources. UG and PGT in-sessional: disciplinary pinpoint expectations, especially in law and history.

guidance.summary: Citation errors undermine verifiability and markers' trust, and automated tools have changed where errors come from. Reference managers and database exports introduce predictable metadata errors, and Walters and Wilder (2023) found that ChatGPT-generated literature reviews contained many fabricated references and frequent errors in genuine ones. Accuracy checking therefore needs two layers: formal matching (citation–reference correspondence, details, consistent style) and fidelity (the cited source actually supports the claim, at the strength claimed).

activities.title: Two-pass check
learnerActions: Pass 1: tick every in-text citation against the reference list, then check the list back against the text
Pass 2: verify the details of five references against the publisher's page or DOI record
Reopen three cited sources and confirm that each claim and its hedging match the source
Record the error types found and the time taken
activities.intendedInsight: Formal accuracy and content fidelity are different checks, and both are needed.
activities.rationale: Separating checks into passes, as in proofreading, reduces cognitive load; the fidelity pass targets misrepresentation of sources, which formatting checks miss.

activities.title: Spot the phantom reference
learnerActions: Receive a reference list mixing accurate references, references with altered details, and non-existent AI-generated references
Search each in a library database, Google Scholar or a DOI resolver
Classify each as accurate, erroneous or non-existent
Discuss why the non-existent ones looked plausible and why no surface cue is reliable on its own
activities.intendedInsight: Plausibility is not existence: references must be checked against an authoritative record.
activities.rationale: Walters and Wilder's findings on fabricated and erroneous AI-generated citations make database checking a necessary habit whenever references come from automated sources.

difficulties.pattern: 'The reference manager formatted it, so it must be right.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Title-case titles, missing editors, wrong item types or duplicate entries in otherwise automated lists.
difficulties.response: Teach the typical errors and how to correct them in the manager's fields rather than only in the document.

difficulties.pattern: Citing from memory or old notes without rechecking the source.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct formats but claims that overstate or misstate the source, or wrong years.
difficulties.response: Build a final fidelity check into the writing schedule and keep page-referenced notes that separate quotation, paraphrase and own comment.

difficulties.pattern: Mixed formats after copying references from different databases and websites.
difficulties.revealedBy: Some entries in the specified style and others in a database's default format.
difficulties.response: Regenerate or retype all entries in one style and add a consistency pass to the checklist.

diagnostic.task: Give a 150-word paragraph with four citations and a five-item reference list containing a missing reference, an uncited entry, a year mismatch and a non-existent reference. Ask the learner to report all problems.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds all four, and checks the suspicious reference in a database before declaring it non-existent.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds the formal mismatches but accepts the non-existent reference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Checks formatting only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on matching and basic details. Pre-sessional courses build systematic pre-submission checks, including reference-manager output. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, fidelity checks matter most in literature-based assignments. PGR writers manage large libraries, switch journal styles and must ensure every attributed claim is supported.
reviewNotes: The fidelity check (does the source support the claim?) slightly extends the skeleton scope note; flagged in authorNotes.

guidance.summary: Petrić (2007) found that high-rated master's theses used citations for a wider range of functions, notably establishing links between sources and comparing the writer's own findings with the literature, whereas low-rated theses relied more on attribution alone. Thompson and Tribble (2001) showed how corpus analysis of citation types can inform teaching, and Hyland (1999) relates citation choices to how writers position themselves in a discipline. Teaching should move learners from 'citation as proof that I read' to 'citation as a move in my argument', using annotated expert and student texts.

activities.title: Function labelling with a typology
learnerActions: Label each citation in an expert literature-review paragraph using a simplified published typology
Compare labels in groups and resolve disagreements by reference to the surrounding argument
Label citations in a higher-rated and a lower-rated student text on the same task
Discuss what the higher-rated writer does with sources that the other does not
activities.intendedInsight: Successful writers use citations to compare, evaluate and connect, not only to attribute.
activities.rationale: Modelled on Petrić's comparison of high- and low-rated theses; analysing student exemplars makes the difference look achievable.

activities.title: Citation forms in a small corpus
learnerActions: Search a small corpus of discipline texts for citation patterns such as author name plus reporting verb and bracketed citations
Classify the results into integral and non-integral types
Note which forms co-occur with evaluation or comparison
Write two sentences of their own using a pattern found for comparison
activities.intendedInsight: Citation forms and functions co-vary, and certain patterns are typical for comparing or evaluating.
activities.rationale: Follows Thompson and Tribble's corpus-based approach to teaching citation.

difficulties.pattern: Source-by-source reporting: 'Smith says… Jones says… Lee says…'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs organised by author with no comparison, evaluation or link to the writer's point.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a normal stage; model reorganising the paragraph around an idea. Avoid simply telling learners to 'be more critical' without showing the moves.

difficulties.pattern: Evaluative reporting verbs used without intending evaluation, for example 'claims' or 'admits' for neutral reporting.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unintended scepticism or criticism in reporting; markers question the writer's stance.
difficulties.response: Map reporting verbs by evaluative force and have learners check whether each verb matches their actual stance.

difficulties.pattern: 'I can't criticise published experts.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Only supportive uses of citation; avoidance of evaluation or comparison.
difficulties.response: Model mitigated evaluation and comparison; show that evaluation can be positive, comparative or about applicability, and that markers expect it.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with five citations and ask the learner to label each citation's function and propose one revision that adds comparison or evaluation.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate labels including functions beyond attribution; the revision adds a genuine comparison or evaluation in an appropriate form.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Labels everything as attribution or support; the revision changes a reporting verb but adds no new function.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish functions.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: introduce a small set of functions in literature-based assignments. PGT: dissertation literature reviews and discussion sections, especially comparing own findings with the literature. PGR: positioning a contribution and managing extensive literatures.
reviewNotes: Petrić's study analysed master's theses in one field; the association between function range and rating should be presented as suggestive rather than universal.

guidance.summary: Hyland's (1999; 2004) corpus studies of research articles across disciplines show systematic differences: the softer disciplines in his corpus tended to cite more densely and to use more direct quotation and integral citation, while the hard sciences and engineering favoured non-integral citation that backgrounds authors. Thompson and Tribble (2001) found differences even between two related agricultural fields in doctoral theses. Learners benefit from investigating their own discipline's practice, while recognising variation within fields and between published and student genres (Nesi & Gardner, 2012).

activities.title: Mini citation study
learnerActions: Select three recent articles from a leading journal in their field
Count citations per 1,000 words in the introductions, the proportion of integral citations and the number of direct quotations
Compare results with a classmate from another discipline
Write three citation guidelines for their own writing
activities.intendedInsight: Citation norms can be discovered empirically and differ by field.
activities.rationale: A learner-as-researcher approach builds transferable genre-analysis habits and grounds advice in the learner's own discipline.

activities.title: Rewrite for another field
learnerActions: Take a paragraph that uses quotations and integral citations
Rewrite it for a hard-science readership using non-integral citation and no direct quotation
Discuss what changes in emphasis and in the image of knowledge
Decide which version suits their own discipline and why
activities.intendedInsight: Citation choices present knowledge either as interpretation attributed to people or as accumulated findings.
activities.rationale: Transformation tasks raise awareness of how form carries disciplinary meaning.

difficulties.pattern: Heavy direct quotation in science or engineering writing because general EAP classes practised quotation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent quotations in lab, design or technical reports.
difficulties.response: Show disciplinary norms with authentic texts and practise paraphrase and non-integral citation.

difficulties.pattern: 'Science never uses integral citation.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Rigid avoidance of naming authors even when contrasting studies or crediting methods.
difficulties.response: Present findings as tendencies and supply counter-examples from the learner's field.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe citation practice in their field and support the description with one example article.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies specific features with evidence from the article and links them to how knowledge is built in the field.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate general features without evidence or explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes generic EAP norms apply everywhere.

guidance.contextNotes: In UG in-sessional work, compare a few features using departmental exemplars. PGT learners, often changing discipline, should analyse their new field's texts early. PGR writers analyse target journals and refine practice for publication.
reviewNotes: Hyland's disciplinary findings derive from research articles; student genres may differ, so learners should also examine discipline-specific student exemplars.

guidance.summary: Learners' mental models of generative AI shape how far they trust it. Bender et al. (2021) characterise large language models as producing fluent text from patterns in training data without grounding in meaning, and warn that training data encode biases and dominant viewpoints; Kasneci et al. (2023) and UNESCO (2023) both identify understanding of these limitations as a prerequisite for responsible educational use. Teaching should give a simple, accurate account of prediction-based generation and then let learners observe characteristic failures for themselves.

activities.title: Predict the failure
learnerActions: Before using a tool, predict which of five questions it will answer unreliably (a reference list on a niche topic, a local fact, a recent event, a definition, an arithmetic problem)
Run the questions and check the answers against sources
Compare predictions with results
Explain each failure in terms of prediction from patterns
activities.intendedInsight: Failures are systematic and predictable, not random glitches.
activities.rationale: Prediction followed by checking builds an accurate mental model better than being told about limitations.

activities.title: Whose view?
learnerActions: Ask a tool the same contested question framed from two perspectives
Compare the answers for framing, examples and omissions
Identify perspectives missing from both
Discuss how training data might explain the pattern
activities.intendedInsight: AI output reflects patterns in its training data, including dominant perspectives.
activities.rationale: Makes the argument about bias in training data concrete and connects it to critical reading.

difficulties.pattern: 'It searches the internet and gives the right answer.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncritical acceptance of output; AI treated as a search engine or database.
difficulties.response: Contrast generation with retrieval using a fabricated reference, and explain that some tools add retrieval but can still misreport what they retrieve.

difficulties.pattern: 'It sounds so confident, so it must be right.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Trusting fluent output, particularly in a second language where the learner cannot easily judge the content.
difficulties.response: Show confident errors; teach that fluency is not evidence and that checking is always needed.

difficulties.pattern: 'AI is useless; it just makes things up.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Wholesale rejection, which leaves learners unable to judge legitimate uses.
difficulties.response: Distinguish tasks where AI is relatively reliable (rephrasing, explaining common concepts) from unreliable ones (specific facts, references).

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Why might an AI tool give you a reference that does not exist?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the model generates plausible text from patterns, so a reference can look correct in form without existing.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says the AI 'makes mistakes' but cannot explain why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Believes the AI looks references up, so they must exist.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: simple accounts and hands-on demonstrations. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific failure modes, such as calculations, code or legal citations. PGR: limits in specialised domains, retrieval-augmented tools and research applications.
reviewNotes: Model capabilities change quickly; examples of failures should be refreshed regularly, but the principle that fluent output needs verification is stable.

guidance.summary: Institutional responses to generative AI vary widely, and many institutions now set permitted use at module or assessment level. Perkins (2023) argued that LLM use does not fit neatly into existing definitions of plagiarism and called for clear, updated policies, while UNESCO (2023) recommends that institutions set and communicate rules on validated, human-centred use. Scales that define levels of permitted AI use for each assessment, such as the AI Assessment Scale (Perkins et al., 2024), make rules more explicit but still require interpretation. Teaching should build a routine — find, read, apply, ask — rather than teach any single policy as fixed.

activities.title: Policy to practice
learnerActions: Read the AI statement in two assessment briefs with different permission levels
Classify ten uses (grammar check, translation, brainstorming, summarising readings, drafting a paragraph and so on) for each brief
Identify uses that are unclear and draft a clarification question
Compare results and discuss why the same use is allowed in one task and not the other
activities.intendedInsight: Permission depends on the task's purpose and wording, and unclear cases should be clarified.
activities.rationale: Applying policies to concrete uses exposes the interpretation that rules require.

activities.title: Spot the hidden AI
learnerActions: List the digital tools they use for writing (editors, translators, grammar checkers, search)
Identify which include generative features
Check whether the policy covers them
Decide what they would declare
activities.intendedInsight: AI features are embedded in common tools and may fall within a policy.
activities.rationale: Learners often do not recognise generative features in familiar tools.

difficulties.pattern: 'My last module allowed it, so this one does too.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uses that were permitted elsewhere appear in work for a module with stricter rules.
difficulties.response: Build a habit of checking the rules for every assessment, for example a checklist item on each brief.

difficulties.pattern: 'Grammar tools and translators aren't AI.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Undeclared use of tools with generative features.
difficulties.response: Show the generative features in common tools and check what the policy says about them.

difficulties.pattern: Fear of asking tutors what is allowed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Guessing, or avoiding all tools including permitted ones.
difficulties.response: Model short clarification emails and normalise asking.

diagnostic.task: Give a brief with an AI statement and ask the learner whether they could use AI to translate their notes from their first language and to check grammar.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Applies the specific wording, identifies any ambiguity, and says what they would declare or ask.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a plausible answer without referring to the wording.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes a single universal rule.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: the course's own policy, with explicit practice. UG and PGT in-sessional: variation between modules and disciplines. PGR: publisher, funder and research ethics policies, as well as the institution's rules for theses.
reviewNotes: Institutional policies change frequently; examples should be refreshed each year. perkins2024aias is a proposed reference.

guidance.summary: Transparency is the common principle across emerging guidance: the ICMJE Recommendations state that AI tools cannot be authors and that their use should be disclosed, and many institutions now ask students to declare AI use. Style guides have issued supplementary guidance on citing AI output (for example the APA Style blog; McAdoo, 2023), which differs between guides. Perkins (2023) argues that clear expectations about acknowledgement are central to integrity in the AI era. Teaching should separate declaring assistance from citing content and build record-keeping into the writing process.

activities.title: Write a proportionate declaration
learnerActions: Read three sample declarations, ranging from vague to detailed
Identify the information each gives (tool, purpose, stage, evaluation)
Write a declaration for their own current assignment
Peer-review for honesty, specificity and proportion
activities.intendedInsight: A good declaration is specific about tool, purpose and stage, and shows the writer's own evaluation.
activities.rationale: Analysis of examples makes the expected content explicit.

activities.title: Process log
learnerActions: Set up a simple log (date, tool, prompt, what was used, what was changed)
Use it during one assignment
Review it to write the declaration
Discuss how it could serve as evidence of their process if questioned
activities.intendedInsight: Records make declarations accurate and protect the writer.
activities.rationale: Logging supports transparency and self-regulation.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I declare it, I'll lose marks.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Under-declaration or vague declarations.
difficulties.response: Explain that permitted, declared use is legitimate and that non-declaration is the risk.

difficulties.pattern: Citing the AI as if it were an authority for claims.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'According to ChatGPT…' used to support academic claims.
difficulties.response: Distinguish acknowledging assistance from evidence; verify claims and cite scholarly sources instead.

difficulties.pattern: Forgetting what was used by the time of submission.
difficulties.revealedBy: Declarations that are incomplete or reconstructed from memory.
difficulties.response: Keep a running log from the start.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a two-sentence declaration for using AI to explain a statistical concept and to check grammar.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specifies tools, purposes, stages and own evaluation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions the tool but not purpose or stage.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Vague or absent.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: simple declarations and logs. UG and PGT in-sessional: module requirements and citation formats. PGR: journal and publisher disclosure statements and authorship norms.
reviewNotes: mcadoo2023 is a proposed reference. Declaration formats vary by institution.

guidance.summary: Walters and Wilder (2023) found that a substantial proportion of the references in literature reviews generated by ChatGPT were fabricated, and that many genuine references contained errors, which makes checking references against authoritative records essential. Wineburg and McGrew (2019) showed that professional fact-checkers verify unfamiliar information by reading laterally rather than judging a page on its own appearance, a strategy that transfers well to AI output. Bender et al. (2021) explain why fluent output is no guarantee of accuracy.

activities.title: Reference reality check
learnerActions: Ask a tool for five references on a topic in their field
Search each in a library database or DOI resolver
Classify each as accurate, erroneous or non-existent
For existing ones, check whether the content matches the AI's description
activities.intendedInsight: AI references must be verified individually, including their content.
activities.rationale: Reproduces Walters and Wilder's finding in the learner's own field.

activities.title: Lateral check of claims
learnerActions: Select two factual claims from an AI answer
Search for independent authoritative sources for each
Compare the claims and their certainty with the sources
Record the verdict and the source used
activities.intendedInsight: Claims are verified by independent sources, not by the output's own confidence.
activities.rationale: Applies lateral reading to AI output.

difficulties.pattern: Checking only that a title 'looks real' or that the authors exist.
difficulties.revealedBy: Real author names attached to non-existent papers pass unnoticed.
difficulties.response: Require a database or DOI match for the whole record, not partial plausibility.

difficulties.pattern: Asking the AI whether its own answer is correct.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'I asked it to check, and it said yes.'
difficulties.response: Explain why self-checking by the same system does not count as independent verification.

difficulties.pattern: Verifying that a reference exists but not what it says.
difficulties.revealedBy: Real references cited for claims they do not support.
difficulties.response: Add a content-matching step to the verification routine.

diagnostic.task: Give three AI-supplied references and ask the learner to verify them in five minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses a database or DOI search, identifies the fabricated and erroneous references, and notes discrepancies in content.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds the fabricated one but misses the erroneous details.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Accepts all three as given.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: reference and fact checks with guided searching. UG and PGT in-sessional: checking summaries and disciplinary claims. PGR: verification within literature reviews and research writing.
reviewNotes: Fabrication rates differ between models and versions; present the finding as a documented risk rather than a fixed rate.

guidance.summary: Kasneci et al. (2023) identify language feedback and personalised practice as promising educational uses of LLMs, alongside the risk of over-reliance. Research on automated writing evaluation suggests that automated feedback works best as one input among others, mediated by teachers and learners' judgement (Stevenson, 2016), and corrective-feedback research suggests that feedback which requires learners to notice and correct their own errors may support longer-term development (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012). Teaching should therefore steer learners towards explanation-seeking uses and checking AI suggestions, not wholesale rewriting.

activities.title: Explain, don't fix
learnerActions: Ask an AI tool to identify, but not correct, errors in a paragraph of their own and to explain the rule involved
Correct the errors themselves
Compare with the tool's correction and evaluate any differences
Record recurring error types in a log
activities.intendedInsight: Locating and explaining errors builds competence in a way that silent correction does not.
activities.rationale: Mirrors indirect corrective feedback, which requires the learner to process the error.

activities.title: Judge the suggestion
learnerActions: Collect ten AI suggestions on their writing
Classify each as accept, reject or modify
Justify decisions with reference to meaning, certainty, register and discipline
Discuss cases where the tool changed meaning or hedging
activities.intendedInsight: AI suggestions can damage meaning and stance and need evaluating.
activities.rationale: Treats AI feedback as one input among others, as recommended for automated writing evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting all suggestions because 'the AI's English is better than mine'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Text that loses the learner's meaning or hedging; no rejected suggestions.
difficulties.response: Show cases where suggestions changed meaning or certainty; frame the learner as the authority on what they mean.

difficulties.pattern: Using AI to rewrite rather than to learn.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assisted texts improve while unassisted writing does not.
difficulties.response: Build in unassisted checks and goal-setting; set explanation-only prompts.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show the prompt they would use to get help with articles in a paragraph without breaching a 'no rewriting' rule.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Asks for errors to be located and explained without corrections, and plans to self-correct.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Asks for corrections but would review them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Asks the tool to rewrite the paragraph.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: guided, explanation-focused uses within course rules. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific language and checking terminology. PGR: editing support within publisher rules, with attention to preserving voice.
reviewNotes: Evidence on the learning effects of generative AI feedback for L2 writers is emerging; the activities are proposals extrapolated from AWE and corrective-feedback research.

guidance.summary: Ivanič (1998) shows how academic writing constructs the writer's identity, and Hyland (2002) how authorial presence is negotiated through specific linguistic choices; AI editing can override these choices, replacing a learner's stance and hedging with generic phrasing. Perkins (2023) raises questions of authorship and the representation of student ability when LLMs are used. Teaching should treat authorship as accountability for ideas, reasoning and words, and help learners notice what AI changes in their texts.

activities.title: Before and after
learnerActions: Ask an AI tool to 'improve' a paragraph of their own
Compare the versions for claims, hedges, boosters, stance and terminology
Mark changes that alter what they meant
Produce a final version that keeps their meaning and voice
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency improvements can come at the cost of meaning and voice.
activities.rationale: Detailed comparison makes changes to stance visible, drawing on research on authorial identity.

activities.title: Where is the line?
learnerActions: Discuss five scenarios of increasing AI involvement
Decide for each whether the work is still the learner's own and why
Relate decisions to what the assessment is meant to show
Write a personal AI-use statement for their programme
activities.intendedInsight: Authorship is about whose reasoning and words are presented, judged against the purpose of the task.
activities.rationale: Builds a principled boundary rather than a list of prohibitions.

difficulties.pattern: 'The ideas are mine, so it doesn't matter who wrote the sentences.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavily AI-written text submitted with a sense of ownership.
difficulties.response: Explain that whether an assessment evidences language as well as ideas depends on its purpose and policy: language-focused tasks usually do, many content tasks may not. Discuss the debate openly, including the equity argument that AI language polishing resembles help from proofreaders or literacy brokers, and refer to the policy for the task.

difficulties.pattern: 'My own English sounds worse, so the AI version represents me better.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to submit own wording; anxiety about language.
difficulties.response: Value the learner's voice as legitimate and show where AI edits changed meaning or stance. Be honest that some readers do react to non-standard English, distinguish changes that improve clarity from those that only make text sound native-like, and point to the criteria actually used for the task.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to compare their paragraph with an AI-edited version and identify one change in stance.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies a specific change in hedging or claim strength and explains its effect.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes stylistic differences only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Prefers the AI version without analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional: the relationship between voice and assessment. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific stance and positioning. PGR: authorship in publications and theses, including disclosure norms.
reviewNotes: Claims about the homogenising effect of AI editing on stance are based on practitioner observation; frame them as a risk to check rather than an established finding.

guidance.summary: Liang et al. (2023) found that several widely used GPT detectors misclassified more than half of a set of TOEFL essays written by non-native English writers as AI-generated, while classifying essays by US eighth-grade students largely correctly, and linked this to the detectors' reliance on measures of textual predictability. Weber-Wulff et al. (2023) found that the detection tools they tested were neither accurate nor reliable. Perkins (2023) cautions against relying on detection. Teaching should make clear that detector output cannot establish misconduct, that the burden of proof lies with the institution, and that keeping ordinary process records is a sensible habit rather than an obligation to prove innocence.

activities.title: What the detector sees
learnerActions: Read a plain-language summary of Liang et al.'s study
Discuss why simpler or more formulaic writing may score as more 'predictable'
Consider what this means for multilingual writers and for fairness
List the evidence a writer could provide of their own process
activities.intendedInsight: Detectors can penalise exactly the writing patterns common in developing L2 writers.
activities.rationale: Directly based on Liang et al.'s findings on detector bias.

activities.title: Build a process trail
learnerActions: Set up version history in their word processor
Keep notes, outlines and drafts for one assignment
Review the trail at the end
Discuss how it could be used if work were questioned
activities.intendedInsight: Process evidence is more informative than detector scores.
activities.rationale: Given detector unreliability, process evidence is the learner's best protection.

difficulties.pattern: 'I must make my writing sound less like AI.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners deliberately complicating their style or using 'humanising' tools.
difficulties.response: Explain detector limits and the integrity and quality risks of such tools; focus on process evidence.

difficulties.pattern: 'The detector proves it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Belief that scores are definitive, among learners and sometimes peers.
difficulties.response: Present the evidence on false positives and the role of human judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Can an AI detector prove that someone used AI?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: No: explains false positives and negatives and the documented bias, and says that human judgement and process evidence matter.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Says detectors are 'not perfect' without explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Says yes.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: reassurance and process evidence, since learners are often anxious. UG and PGT in-sessional: understanding institutional processes. PGR: implications for theses and publications.
reviewNotes: Detection technology and institutional use change; weberwulff2023 is a proposed reference. Institutions differ in whether they use detectors at all.

guidance.summary: Kasneci et al. (2023) and UNESCO (2023) both stress that the educational value of generative AI depends on use that supports learners' own thinking rather than substituting for it. Self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002) offers a frame: prompting for learning means setting a goal, monitoring understanding during the interaction and evaluating afterwards without the tool. Teaching should contrast learning-oriented and output-oriented prompts and build in unassisted checks.

activities.title: Two prompts, two outcomes
learnerActions: Write an output prompt and a learning prompt for the same task
Run both and compare what they would learn from each
Explain the concept afterwards without the tool
Refine the learning prompt
activities.intendedInsight: The same tool can replace or support thinking depending on the prompt.
activities.rationale: Contrast makes the difference concrete; the unassisted explanation tests learning.

activities.title: Sparring partner
learnerActions: Ask a tool to question them Socratically on a reading
Answer without looking at the text
Ask for counter-arguments to their position
Write a short reflection on what they learned
activities.intendedInsight: AI can provide questioning and challenge that support understanding.
activities.rationale: Questioning and retrieval support learning; the reflection supports self-evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Prompts that ask for answers or finished text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot explain content they 'studied' with AI.
difficulties.response: Teach learning-oriented prompt patterns and unassisted checks.

difficulties.pattern: Accepting a too-advanced or generic explanation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report confusion but do not iterate.
difficulties.response: Model iteration: specifying level, examples and the learner's current understanding.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a prompt to help them understand a difficult concept from a lecture.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Specifies level, asks for explanation and questions, and includes a self-test.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Asks for an explanation without constraints or a follow-up.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Asks for a summary or answer to submit.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: structured prompt patterns linked to course content. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific learning uses within module rules. PGR: using AI to test arguments and explore unfamiliar fields.
reviewNotes: Evidence on learning outcomes from AI-supported study is emerging and mixed; activities are proposals.

guidance.summary: AI-based discovery and summarisation tools can speed up orientation to a literature, but their coverage, ranking and reproducibility are often opaque. Walters and Wilder's (2023) findings on fabricated and erroneous citations show the need to verify, and UNESCO (2023) emphasises human judgement and validation in research uses. Teaching should position these tools as finding aids alongside documented database searching and reading of full texts.

activities.title: Tool versus database
learnerActions: Run the same question through an AI discovery tool and a subject database
Compare the results for overlap, missing key papers and ranking
Document both searches
Discuss implications for a literature review
activities.intendedInsight: AI tools find some leads but miss others and are hard to reproduce.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison shows the limits of coverage and the need for documented searching.

activities.title: Summary audit
learnerActions: Obtain an AI summary of a paper
Read the paper
Mark errors, omissions and changes in certainty in the summary
Write their own summary
activities.intendedInsight: AI summaries can misrepresent findings and certainty.
activities.rationale: Verification against the full text is essential before citing.

difficulties.pattern: Citing papers from AI summaries without reading them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misrepresented findings; citations of papers the learner cannot discuss.
difficulties.response: Require reading of cited papers and spot-check discussion.

difficulties.pattern: 'The tool found everything relevant.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Literature reviews missing key works in the field.
difficulties.response: Compare with database searches and citation chaining.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would use an AI research tool in a dissertation literature review.
diagnostic.strongResponse: As a finding aid alongside documented database searches, with verification and full-text reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions verification but would rely on the tool's summaries.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would use the tool to write the review.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: orientation uses with verification. PGT: dissertation literature searching and documentation. PGR: systematic and scoping reviews, where reproducibility requirements may limit AI use.
reviewNotes: Specific tools change rapidly; teaching should avoid product-specific claims.

guidance.summary: UNESCO (2023) and Kasneci et al. (2023) both highlight data privacy and intellectual property as central concerns in educational and research uses of generative AI. Inputs to public tools may be retained or used for training depending on the terms, and the ICMJE Recommendations ask reviewers not to upload manuscripts to tools where confidentiality cannot be assured. Teaching should give learners a checklist for uploading decisions grounded in their institution's policies and ethics approvals.

activities.title: Upload or not?
learnerActions: Classify ten items (own draft, published article PDF, interview transcript, a peer's essay, anonymised survey data and so on) as safe to upload, upload only with conditions, or do not upload
Justify each with reference to consent, copyright, confidentiality and the tool's terms
Compare with institutional guidance
Draft a personal checklist
activities.intendedInsight: Uploading decisions depend on whose data it is, what permission exists and what the tool does with it.
activities.rationale: Scenario-based classification makes abstract principles actionable.

activities.title: Read the terms
learnerActions: Locate the data-use terms of a commonly used AI tool
Identify statements about retention and training
Compare with an institutionally licensed tool if available
Summarise the implications for coursework and research
activities.intendedInsight: Tools differ in how they handle data, and terms matter.
activities.rationale: Builds the habit of checking terms before use.

difficulties.pattern: 'It's anonymised enough if I remove the names.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcripts with identifying details uploaded.
difficulties.response: Explain indirect identifiers and the need to follow ethics approvals.

difficulties.pattern: 'Published articles are public, so I can upload them anywhere.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uploading licensed PDFs without checking terms.
difficulties.response: Explain licences and access terms and check institutional guidance.

diagnostic.task: Ask whether a learner may upload a classmate's draft to an AI tool to get feedback for them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: No, not without consent and attention to the tool's terms and course rules; suggests alternatives.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sees a problem but cannot say why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problem.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: uploading readings and peers' work. PGT: dissertation data and ethics. PGR: research data, peer review confidentiality and intellectual property in publications and patents.
reviewNotes: Legal positions on copyright and AI differ by jurisdiction and are changing; avoid presenting them as settled.

guidance.summary: The ICAI (2021) frames academic integrity as a commitment to six fundamental values — honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage — and the Handbook of Academic Integrity (Bretag, 2016) documents a sector shift from purely punitive approaches towards education and shared responsibility. For learners entering an unfamiliar academic system, values give a rationale for conventions that can otherwise seem arbitrary. Teaching should connect values to concrete practices and realistic dilemmas rather than present them as abstract virtues.

activities.title: From values to practices
learnerActions: Match each of the six values to two concrete academic practices (for example, respect: representing other writers accurately; courage: raising a problem in a group)
Rank five integrity dilemmas by difficulty and identify the competing values in each
Discuss what a person acting with integrity would do and what support would make that easier
Write a short personal statement of integrity commitments for the course
activities.intendedInsight: Integrity is enacted through everyday choices, often under competing pressures.
activities.rationale: Follows the ICAI values model and the educative approach in the integrity literature; dilemmas move learners beyond agreeing with abstract statements.

activities.title: Who is affected?
learnerActions: Read a misconduct scenario such as falsified lab results in a group report
Map who is affected: the student, peers, the institution, future patients or clients, the field
Identify which values are breached for each
Propose the honest alternative at each decision point
activities.intendedInsight: Misconduct has consequences beyond one person's grade.
activities.rationale: Consequence mapping makes trust and fairness concrete and connects integrity to professional futures.

difficulties.pattern: 'Integrity is just the university's system for catching us.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Cynical or anxious responses; questions focus on detection and penalties.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the regulatory side honestly but lead with community purposes and available support. Avoid opening a course with sanctions and case horror stories, which raise anxiety without building understanding.

difficulties.pattern: 'Helping a friend with their assignment is the right thing to do.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Endorsing sharing of work out of loyalty or kindness in scenario discussions.
difficulties.response: Treat it as a genuine conflict between loyalty and fairness, and explore ways to help (explaining concepts, pointing to support) that do not put the friend at risk.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, with an example, how one of the six values applies to writing an essay from sources.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a value, links it to a specific practice and explains how others rely on that practice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names a value with a generic example and little explanation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot link values to practice, or equates integrity with not getting caught.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introduce early and positively, linked to the course's own expectations. UG and PGT in-sessional: link to professional codes in the discipline, such as health or engineering. PGR: connect to research integrity and responsibilities to participants and the field.

guidance.summary: Research on second-language source use complicates simple definitions of plagiarism. Howard (1995) proposed patchwriting as a developmental strategy distinct from cheating; Pecorari (2003; 2008) showed that postgraduate L2 writers' unattributed source language typically lacked any intention to deceive; and Shi (2004) found that how much students borrowed without attribution varied with the writing task. Pennycook (1996) traced how notions of textual ownership are historically and institutionally situated, an argument that should not be turned into claims that any national or cultural group 'does not understand' plagiarism. Teaching should make the textual criteria explicit, separate development from deception, and still be clear about what institutions require.

activities.title: Continuum of source use
learnerActions: Place six versions of a source-based paragraph on a continuum from appropriate to plagiarised
Justify each placement with reference to wording, ideas, structure and acknowledgement
Compare the placements with the institution's definition
Revise the two weakest versions
activities.intendedInsight: Plagiarism concerns ideas and structure as well as wording, and a citation does not license copied language.
activities.rationale: Pecorari's analysis separates the textual features of source use from the writer's intention; a continuum makes those features visible without equating every problem with cheating.

activities.title: Why do conventions differ?
learnerActions: Read short accounts of memorisation, imitation and textual borrowing in different historical and educational settings
Discuss what purpose each practice served in its setting
Identify what the current institution expects and why
Write advice for a new student that explains these expectations without judging previous practices
activities.intendedInsight: Different conventions serve different purposes; current expectations can be learned without devaluing prior education.
activities.rationale: Pennycook's analysis supports discussing textual ownership as situated; framing differences around educational practices rather than nationality avoids essentialising learners.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I cite the source, I can use its sentences.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Cited but unquoted strings of source wording; surprise at feedback.
difficulties.response: Show the double requirement: citation for the source of ideas, quotation marks for borrowed wording. Work with the learner's own text.

difficulties.pattern: 'I changed some words, so it's my paraphrase.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Synonym substitution with the source's sentence structure retained (patchwriting).
difficulties.response: Treat this as a stage: teach reading for understanding and writing from notes with the source closed. Do not use misconduct framing or punitive language for a first developmental instance, but do state the institutional standard clearly.

difficulties.pattern: 'Plagiarism only means copying words.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Uncited borrowing of a source's argument structure, examples or data.
difficulties.response: Use paired examples of idea and structure borrowing with and without attribution.

diagnostic.task: Show a cited but patchwritten paragraph and ask whether it is acceptable and why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies retained wording and structure despite the citation, explains the need for quotation or genuine paraphrase, and distinguishes a developmental problem from deception.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a problem but cannot specify it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges it acceptable because it is cited.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: clear, non-threatening definitions with many examples and plenty of formative practice. UG and PGT in-sessional: discipline-specific forms such as code, data and images. PGR: authorship and idea attribution in collaborative research, and the standards applied to theses and publications.
reviewNotes: Whether intention bears on whether something counts as plagiarism, as opposed to the penalty, is contested and handled differently across institutions.

guidance.summary: Learners are often surprised that reusing their own work can be misconduct. In coursework the issue is assessment validity — each assessment should evidence new learning — and institutions differ in what they allow. In research writing, the ICMJE Recommendations require disclosure of overlapping publications, while some reuse of text (for example methods descriptions) may be acceptable with transparency; Bretag and Mahmud (2009) argue for distinguishing self-plagiarism from appropriate textual re-use. Teaching should centre on transparency and consulting the relevant policy.

activities.title: Reuse scenarios
learnerActions: Read four reuse scenarios ranging from coursework to publication
Find the relevant rule in the programme regulations or a journal's policy for each
Decide what must be disclosed, cited or permitted
Draft the sentence that discloses or cites the earlier work
activities.intendedInsight: Reuse is judged by the purpose of the new work and by transparency, not by whose words they are.
activities.rationale: Scenario work against actual policies builds the habit of checking rules rather than relying on intuition about ownership.

activities.title: Thesis to article (PGR)
learnerActions: Identify a thesis chapter or conference paper that could become an article
Check the target journal's policy on prior dissemination, preprints and deposited theses
Draft a cover-letter disclosure of related outputs
Discuss with a supervisor what counts as substantial new contribution
activities.intendedInsight: Moving work between genres is normal but requires disclosure and policy checks.
activities.rationale: Disclosure of related publications is a standard editorial requirement, and early-career researchers often do not know how to make it.

difficulties.pattern: 'It's my work, so I can use it however I like.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs from earlier assessed work reused without acknowledgement.
difficulties.response: Explain the assessment-validity rationale: the same work cannot evidence learning twice. Show how to build on earlier work by citing it, with permission where needed.

difficulties.pattern: 'I rewrote it a bit, so it counts as new.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Lightly revised versions of earlier assignments submitted as new work.
difficulties.response: Distinguish revision of wording from new analysis or contribution; refer to the regulations.

difficulties.pattern: Uncertainty about whether conference papers, preprints or deposited theses count as prior publication.
difficulties.revealedBy: PGR writers either over-worry or fail to disclose related outputs.
difficulties.response: Show that policies differ by journal and field, and model checking author guidelines and asking editors.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Can you use material from your previous essay in this assignment?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Says it depends on the regulations and the brief, refers to permission and self-citation, and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows there are limits but cannot say where to check.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Assumes reuse is always acceptable because the work is their own.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: resubmission rules, especially for students repeating modules or moving from foundation or pre-sessional programmes. PGT: reuse between assignments and the dissertation. PGR: text recycling in theses by publication, articles and grant applications.
reviewNotes: bretagmahmud2009 is a proposed reference and must be verified before publication.

guidance.summary: Collusion is the integrity area in which learners' intentions are most often cooperative and in which the rules vary most between assessments. Bretag et al.'s (2014) student survey points to students' wish to be taught explicitly what is expected, and the integrity literature (Bretag, 2016) emphasises clear communication of collaboration boundaries. Teaching should use the actual assessment brief, present boundary scenarios, and frame legitimate collaboration positively so that learners do not withdraw from beneficial peer learning.

activities.title: Traffic-light scenarios
learnerActions: Read an assessment brief and its collaboration rules
Classify ten scenarios as green (permitted), amber (permitted if acknowledged or limited) or red (collusion)
Discuss disagreements and identify the information that would resolve them
Compare classifications under a different brief that permits group work
activities.intendedInsight: The same behaviour can be legitimate or collusive depending on the assessment's rules.
activities.rationale: Applying rules to scenarios makes tacit boundaries explicit, as students in the integrity literature request.

activities.title: Saying no and asking
learnerActions: Draft a friendly message declining a friend's request to see a finished essay, offering an alternative form of help
Draft a short email asking a tutor whether a particular kind of collaboration is allowed
Peer-review both for tone and clarity
Role-play the conversation
activities.intendedInsight: Protecting integrity can be done kindly and without damaging relationships.
activities.rationale: Learners often know the rule but lack the language to act on it in peer relationships.

difficulties.pattern: 'Sharing my essay is just helping; my friend won't copy it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Finished work shared 'for reference', with both students subsequently implicated.
difficulties.response: Show that both parties are usually treated as involved and that intention to help does not change what is submitted.

difficulties.pattern: 'In my previous studies we did homework together and handed in the same answers.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Identical answers or code in individual submissions.
difficulties.response: Validate collaborative learning, then distinguish discussing approaches from submitting shared answers in individually assessed work.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding all discussion with peers for fear of collusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners decline study groups or peer review; isolation.
difficulties.response: Present legitimate collaboration positively and show the many permitted forms.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'You and a classmate discussed the essay question together. What can you share and what must you do separately?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes discussing ideas and sources from writing or sharing text, refers to the brief, and mentions acknowledging significant input where required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a general distinction but cannot apply it to specific cases.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Believes any shared work is fine if both understand it, or that any discussion is forbidden.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introduce through course tasks, since study groups are encouraged. UG in-sessional: lab reports, problem sets and code are the most frequent risk areas. PGT: group assessments with individual components and the boundary between them.

guidance.summary: Survey research by Bretag et al. (2019) associated contract cheating with students' perceptions that there were many opportunities to cheat and with dissatisfaction with the teaching and learning environment, which suggests addressing conditions and support rather than blaming particular groups. Newton's (2018) systematic review suggests that self-reported rates of commercial contract cheating have risen over time. Providers market directly to students, including through social media and messaging channels, so teaching should cover how to recognise their tactics and the legitimate routes to help.

activities.title: Deconstructing an advertisement
learnerActions: Analyse a constructed advertisement for 'model essays' and its language (guarantees, urgency, reassurance)
Identify what is actually being sold and what the terms omit
List the risks to the buyer, including data misuse and blackmail
Rewrite the advert as an honest description
activities.intendedInsight: Marketing language disguises outsourcing and hides the risks to the student.
activities.rationale: Critical reading of persuasive texts is an EAP skill in its own right and inoculates learners against approaches they are likely to receive.

activities.title: Map the alternatives
learnerActions: List the support services available on their course and how to access them
Match each problem a student might have (time, language, understanding the task) to a service
Find the institution's rules on proofreading and editing support
Share the map with the class
activities.intendedInsight: Most problems that lead to outsourcing have a legitimate solution if addressed early.
activities.rationale: Associations between contract cheating and dissatisfaction with the learning environment suggest that visible, accessible support is part of prevention.

difficulties.pattern: 'A model essay is just for reference, so buying one isn't cheating.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Bought 'model' essays submitted or closely adapted.
difficulties.response: Explain that submitting or adapting outsourced work is contract cheating regardless of what the provider calls it.

difficulties.pattern: 'My cousin wrote it for free, so that's not contract cheating.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Unpaid third-party authorship, including heavy 'editing' by others.
difficulties.response: Clarify that payment is not the criterion; authorship of the submitted work is.

difficulties.pattern: Desperation close to a deadline.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report receiving or considering offers when overwhelmed.
difficulties.response: Normalise asking for help and give concrete routes, including extensions. Avoid fear-only messaging, which does not address the underlying pressure.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'A website offers you a custom essay written by an expert. What are the risks, and what could you do instead?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies academic, legal or financial, and blackmail and data risks, and names specific alternatives.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies academic penalties only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problem if the essay is 'original'.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: address early, as students may be contacted by providers soon after arrival. UG and PGT in-sessional: high-stakes periods such as dissertations and resits. In England, providing or advertising contract cheating services to students was made a criminal offence by the Skills and Post-16 Education Act 2022, and several other jurisdictions have similar laws; the legal position varies by country.
reviewNotes: bretag2019 and newton2018 are proposed references and must be verified. The blackmail risk is widely reported in sector guidance but currently has no listed source; add one (for example QAA guidance on contract cheating) before publication. Verify the legislative statement and jurisdictions before publication.

guidance.summary: Text-matching tools compare submissions with indexed sources and report overlaps; they do not identify plagiarism, cannot reliably detect paraphrased, translated or outsourced work, and include many legitimate matches. Pecorari (2013) cautions against letting software define good source use, and the Handbook of Academic Integrity (Bretag, 2016) stresses academic judgement in interpreting reports. Where institutions let students see formative reports, these can support learning about source use if learners are taught to read the matches rather than chase a percentage.

activities.title: Read the report, not the number
learnerActions: Examine two sample reports, one with a high percentage made up mainly of cited quotations and references and one with a low percentage hiding an uncited patchwrite
Classify each highlighted match by type
Decide which report shows a real problem
Explain why the overall percentage is misleading
activities.intendedInsight: The percentage carries no verdict; only interpretation of specific matches does.
activities.rationale: Directly counters the belief that a threshold separates plagiarism from originality.

activities.title: Fix the source use, not the match
learnerActions: Take a flagged patchwritten passage from a formative report
Reread the source, close it, and note its main idea in their own words
Rewrite the passage from the notes and add the citation
Compare with a version produced by synonym substitution and discuss the difference in quality
activities.intendedInsight: Revising from understanding produces better writing, whereas rewording to lower a score produces worse writing and may still be plagiarism.
activities.rationale: Patchwriting is best addressed by developing reading-to-write processes rather than by surface rewording.

difficulties.pattern: 'My score is under 15%, so I'm safe.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners citing a numeric threshold; no review of individual matches.
difficulties.response: Explain that there is no universal threshold and that a low score can hide problems; review matches together.

difficulties.pattern: Changing words or using paraphrasing tools until the highlighting disappears.
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward synonym-substituted text, sometimes with distorted meaning.
difficulties.response: Show the quality cost and the integrity risk, and teach rewriting from understanding.

difficulties.pattern: Panic at any highlighted text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Anxious questions about correctly quoted and referenced material being highlighted.
difficulties.response: Show that quotations, reference entries and common phrases are expected matches.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Your report says 35%. Is that plagiarism?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Says it depends on what the matches are, explains how to check them, and notes that people, not software, decide.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows a percentage is not a verdict but cannot explain how to interpret matches.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the percentage as a verdict.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: formative use of reports where permitted, with teacher-guided interpretation. UG and PGT in-sessional: department practices and understanding what happens when a report raises concern. PGR: thesis and publication screening, including matches to the writer's own earlier outputs.
reviewNotes: Institutions differ in whether students may view reports before final submission and in how reports are used.

guidance.summary: Learners often discover integrity procedures only when facing a concern about their work, when anxiety and unfamiliar terminology can lead to poor decisions. Bretag et al. (2014) found variation in students' awareness of integrity policy and support and argued for educative approaches, and making the process explicit is part of that education. Because procedures, terminology and outcomes vary between institutions, teaching should be built around the learner's own institution's documents and support services.

activities.title: Policy scavenger hunt
learnerActions: Locate the institution's integrity policy and a module's assessment rules
Find answers to set questions: definitions, stages, who decides, possible outcomes, rights to support and appeal
Summarise the process as a flowchart
Compare flowcharts in groups and correct errors
activities.intendedInsight: The process is knowable, staged and includes rights and support.
activities.rationale: Explicit engagement with the real policy addresses the uneven policy awareness reported in survey research.

activities.title: Responding to a meeting invitation
learnerActions: Read a constructed invitation letter
Identify the concern, the deadline and the support available
List evidence of their writing process that could be relevant (notes, drafts, version history)
Draft a short, factual reply confirming attendance and requesting any needed information
activities.intendedInsight: A calm, prompt and factual response, with support, is in the student's interest.
activities.rationale: Rehearsing the genre before it is needed is intended to reduce anxiety and support appropriate formality (a practitioner proposal); Bretag (2016) is cited for the educative approach to integrity, not for this effect.

difficulties.pattern: Ignoring or delaying a response out of fear.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missed deadlines in the process; reports of avoiding email.
difficulties.response: Normalise seeking advice early and show where independent advice is available.

difficulties.pattern: 'The software has already decided I'm guilty.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Belief that a similarity or AI-detection score is the verdict.
difficulties.response: Explain the role of academic judgement and the evidence considered in the process.

difficulties.pattern: Writing an over-apologetic admission or an aggressive denial.
difficulties.revealedBy: Draft replies with inappropriate tone or claims not supported by evidence.
difficulties.response: Model a factual, courteous register and advise seeking support before writing statements.
