diagnostic.task: Ask: 'Where would you find your institution's academic integrity policy, and what are the main stages if a concern is raised?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates the policy and summarises its stages, support and appeal rights accurately.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows the policy exists but describes the process vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know where the policy is or assumes outcomes are automatic.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: overview of the process and support, with emphasis on prevention and on how the next institution's policy may differ. UG and PGT in-sessional: module-level rules and processes. PGR: research misconduct procedures, which are usually separate from student misconduct procedures.
reviewNotes: Terminology (for example 'academic misconduct', 'poor academic practice') and procedures vary substantially between institutions; examples should be localised.

guidance.summary: Integrity breaches are often decisions made under acute pressure rather than planned deception. Bretag et al. (2019) associated contract cheating with perceived opportunity and dissatisfaction with the teaching and learning environment, which points to conditions and support as levers for prevention. Self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002) supports the planning and monitoring that reduce the crises in which shortcuts become tempting. Teaching should normalise asking for extensions and support and make procedures concrete before learners need them.

activities.title: Deadline map
learnerActions: Map all assessment deadlines for the term on one calendar
Identify clusters and back-plan milestones
Mark the extension and extenuating-circumstances deadlines and procedures
Identify one support service to contact at each risk point
activities.intendedInsight: Many crises are predictable and can be prevented or managed through procedures.
activities.rationale: Forethought and planning are core phases of self-regulated learning.

activities.title: Write the email now
learnerActions: Draft an extension request for a realistic scenario
Peer-review for clarity, mitigation and evidence
Save it as a template
Discuss what makes requesting help difficult and how to overcome it
activities.intendedInsight: Requesting help is a normal, procedural act.
activities.rationale: Preparing the request in advance lowers the barrier to using legitimate options when pressure arrives.

difficulties.pattern: 'Asking for an extension shows weakness or will lower my grade.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners do not seek extensions even when eligible.
difficulties.response: Explain the procedures and that eligible requests are routine; share anonymised examples.

difficulties.pattern: Not knowing that extenuating-circumstances processes exist, or missing their deadlines.
difficulties.revealedBy: Late claims; surprise that support was available.
difficulties.response: Teach the procedures explicitly early in the course.

difficulties.pattern: Starting assignments too late and finishing under extreme time pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Work submitted at the deadline; patterns of late-night drafting.
difficulties.response: Use milestone planning and check-ins; avoid moralising, which does not change planning behaviour.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'If you were ill the week before a deadline, what exactly would you do and by when?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the specific procedure, evidence, deadline and contact.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Would email the tutor but does not know the formal procedure.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Would try to finish somehow or does not know any options.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional: introduce procedures early; pre-sessional deadlines are intense and progression stakes are high. UG and PGT in-sessional: dissertation periods, part-time work and caring responsibilities. PGR: long-term workload, supervision relationships and wellbeing.
reviewNotes: bretag2019 is a proposed reference; the summary of its findings should be checked against the article.

guidance.summary: Fanelli's (2009) meta-analysis of survey data found that about 2% of scientists admitted fabricating or falsifying data at least once and up to about a third admitted other questionable research practices, with higher rates reported for colleagues' behaviour. For research students the main risks are rarely outright fabrication but undisclosed analytic flexibility, poor record-keeping and authorship disputes. Teaching should use discipline-relevant cases, link to codes of conduct such as the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, institutional and funder codes and, in medicine, the ICMJE Recommendations, and emphasise transparent reporting.

activities.title: Grey-zone cases
learnerActions: Read four short cases from their discipline (data exclusion, image adjustment, selective citation, authorship order)
Classify each as acceptable, a questionable practice or misconduct
Identify the relevant code of conduct provision
Propose transparent alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Most integrity risks lie in grey zones where transparency is the remedy.
activities.rationale: Fanelli's findings show questionable practices are far more common than fabrication, so teaching should focus on them.

activities.title: Data trail audit
learnerActions: Map how one result in their own project moves from raw data to the reported figure
Identify where records, versions or decisions are missing
Set up a simple versioning and record-keeping system
Write a transparent methods note on any exclusions or deviations
activities.intendedInsight: Good records make results checkable and protect the researcher.
activities.rationale: Verifiability depends on documented data handling.

difficulties.pattern: 'Removing data that doesn't fit is just cleaning.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Undocumented exclusions; results that change after exclusion.
difficulties.response: Distinguish pre-specified, justified exclusion from outcome-driven exclusion, and require reporting of both.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to question a supervisor's or senior colleague's practice.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report discomfort but take no action.
difficulties.response: Discuss courage as an integrity value and identify confidential advice routes.

difficulties.pattern: 'Research integrity just means not plagiarising.'
difficulties.revealedBy: No awareness of fabrication, falsification or questionable practices.
difficulties.response: Introduce fabrication, falsification and questionable practices with field examples.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain the difference between falsification and a questionable research practice, with an example from their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate distinction with a field-specific example and a transparent alternative.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Defines falsification but cannot identify questionable practices.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates research integrity with avoiding plagiarism.

guidance.contextNotes: UG in-sessional: lab reports and final-year projects (honest reporting of results, including failed experiments). PGT: dissertation data and ethics. PGR: full codes of conduct, data management plans and publication ethics.
reviewNotes: allea2023 is a proposed reference and must be verified.

authorNotes: cit.why-cite overlaps heavily with src.source-functions, and src.source-functions overlaps with cit.citation-functions. I scoped cit.why-cite as the rationale for citing (B1 entry point), src.source-functions as a prerequisite of cit.citation-functions, and cit.citation-functions as the advanced analytic typology (Petrić-style). Consider merging cit.why-cite and src.source-functions, or rescoping src.source-functions explicitly as 'what sources do in my paragraph'.

Assumed edge directions that other groups must not reverse (to avoid global cycles): src.quoting -> cit.locators; src.source-functions, src.citation-forms and src.reporting-verbs -> cit.citation-functions; dig.reference-managers and edt.proofreading -> cit.accuracy-consistency; voc.abbreviations-latin -> cit.author-date-in-text; sen.capitalisation and inf.source-types -> cit.reference-list; inf.scholarly-communication -> cit.diverse-sources.

cit.accuracy-consistency: I extended the scope to include fidelity (the cited source actually supports the claim). Content fidelity of citation is otherwise not covered anywhere in the skeleton and is increasingly important with AI-generated text.

reg.disciplinary-style lists citation among its features, overlapping with cit.disciplinary-citation; I did not link them to avoid a likely cycle. Suggest reg.disciplinary-style stays a broad overview and points to cit.disciplinary-citation as a related, not prerequisite, topic.
src.secondary-citation is a citation-mechanics topic and arguably belongs in CIT; it is left in SRC but covered in cit.author-date-in-text mastery evidence.

Gap: there is no topic on attribution in multimodal and spoken work (image credits, licences such as Creative Commons, citing on slides and posters). dat.captions-labelling and sem.citing-in-speech cover parts of this. Suggest a topic such as 'Attribution in slides, posters and multimodal work'.

cit.diverse-sources and gai.acknowledging-use both cover citation of AI output. I scoped cit.diverse-sources to the reference format for AI output as one non-recoverable source type, and gai.acknowledging-use to declarations, records and policy compliance.
gai.prompting-for-learning and gai.language-support overlap. I scoped prompting-for-learning as the general technique (prerequisite) and language-support as its application to language development.
gai.detection-limits is closely tied to INT; it is placed in GAI per the skeleton and linked to int.similarity-reports as a soft prerequisite.

Gap: AI paraphrasing and 'humanising' tools (and paraphrasing/rewording tools generally) are a major integrity issue for EAP learners but have no clear home between dig.machine-translation, gai.policies and src.paraphrasing. Suggest a scope note on gai.policies or a new topic.

Assumed edge directions that other groups must not reverse: wpr.task-analysis, fbk.assessment-literacy -> gai.policies; inf.lateral-reading, inf.databases -> gai.verifying-output; fbk.corrective-feedback -> gai.language-support; sta.authorial-voice -> gai.authorship-voice; src.summarising-text, rdc.literature-mapping -> gai.research-tools; inf.open-access -> gai.privacy-ip; lrn.self-regulation -> gai.prompting-for-learning. dig.machine-translation and dig.automated-feedback-tools may take GAI topics as prerequisites but should not be prerequisites of gai.how-genai-works.

int.plagiarism scope note mentions 'culturally situated views of textual ownership'. I have framed this through historical and educational practices (Pennycook, 1996) rather than national cultures, to avoid essentialising; reviewers should keep that framing.

Gap: no topic covers integrity in examinations and online assessment (unauthorised materials, impersonation, sharing questions during take-home exams). exm.open-book touches this. Suggest a scope extension of int.collusion or a new INT topic.

Gap: uploading lecture materials or others' work to note-sharing and file-exchange sites (a common route into both collusion and copyright breach) has no clear home; it is mentioned under int.contract-cheating.

int.recycling-own-work overlaps with pub.authorship and pub.publishing-process for PGR (redundant publication, thesis-by-publication). I left no edge to PUB to keep the topic usable for UG and PGT; PUB topics could take int.recycling-own-work as a prerequisite.

edt.proofreading-ethics is closely related to int.contract-cheating (editing that rewrites content is a key grey area). I did not add an edge in either direction; the integrating editor should choose one direction (I would suggest int.contract-cheating -> edt.proofreading-ethics as soft, or the reverse, but not both).

Assumed edge directions that other groups must not reverse: src.patchwriting -> int.similarity-reports; lrn.support-services, lrn.time-management and prg.requests -> int.pressure-risks; fbk.assessment-literacy -> int.collusion and int.recycling-own-work; grw.purposes -> int.collusion; voc.university-terminology -> int.policy-processes.
